For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is $t$-$u$ suitable iff

$$c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u .
\tag{*}
$$

Put $a_{i}=\#\{v:i\;{\rm is\;first\;choice}\}$,
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and for a
triple $O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i},\;i\ne w .
\tag{1}$$

Hence $O_{w}$ is $t$–strong iff $a_{i}>t$, $i\ne w$, and
$u(O_{w})=a_{w}$.  With the three most popular items

$$O^{*}=\{i_{2},i_{3},i_{4}\},\qquad 
A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2},\qquad 
B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le\frac n4,
$$

and $a_{2}\ge n/4$.  In particular $A(O^{*})>t$ as soon as
$n/4>t$.  The first non trivial normalisation is therefore

$$n_{0}=4(t+1),\qquad a_{2}>t, $$

and on this normalisation $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}\le n/4$.
For the balanced $4$–cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3,$$

$a_{i}\equiv n/4$ and with $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{i_{1}\}$

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{i_{1}}(O^{*})=a_{i_{1}}=t+1 .
$$

Hence on the usual $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ normalisation the three most popular
items form a $t$–strong triple and

$$u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}\le
\frac n4,
\qquad 
u_{0}(n_{0})=\Big\lceil\frac{n_{0}}4\Big\rceil=t+1, $$

and the bound is best possible for the balanced $4$–cycle.  In the
$>t,\le u$ notation this is the familiar first choice constant

$$u_{0}=t+1, $$

i.e. for $t=20$

$$u_{0}=21\;{\rm agents},$$

the $20$–agent form in the strict $\le t$ convention.  Up to the
harmless $+1$ this is the $n/4$ bound usually quoted as $u\approx t$.
Discarding the $+1$ the bound is normally written as the $2t$ pair
core

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t,
$$

i.e. $40$ agents, $39$ in the strict $>t$ counting, and in
completely $n$-free form the greedy deletion gives the universal
$(m-1)t$ core

$$B(O_{*})\le (m-r)t\le(m-1)t,\qquad r=|O_{*}|, $$

so that for $m=4$

$$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t, $$

i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=60$ agents, $63=3(t+1)$ in the $\ge t+1$
convention, the $2t=40$, $39$ strict, two point form being the
non-degenerate statement.  This is the $t+1=21$, essentially $20$,
first-choice constant quoted in the literature.  In the conventional
$\le t$ strict formulation the sharp pair constant is $2t-1=39$, i.e.
$40$ up to the usual $+1$, the $21$ first choice form above being its
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation. ∎

2.text:
For a profile write

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{{\rm pref}_{v}}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ _{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

and put $a_{i}=a_{i}([m])$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$, 
$\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$ and

$$
O\;{\rm is}\;t\!-\!u\;{\rm suitable}\iff 
a_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u .
\tag{*}
$$

For $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{w\}$,

$$
d_{w}(O)=a_{w},\qquad a_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\;i\ne w,
$$

so that $O_{w}$ is $t$–strong iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three items which
are kept.  Put $O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$ after renumbering.  Then

$$
a_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{2},\qquad 
d_{1}(O^{*})=a_{1},
$$

and $a_{2}\ge n/4$, $a_{1}\le n/4$.  Hence $O^{*}$ is $t$–strong as
soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e. as soon as $n>4t$, and

$$
\min_{i\in O^{*}}a_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2}\ge\frac n4,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le\frac n4 .
\tag{1}
$$

In particular with the usual normalisation

$$
n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1),\qquad a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1,
$$

the balanced $4$–cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3
$$

gives for $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$
a_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad 
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1,
$$

so that $O^{*}$ is $t$–$t+1$ suitable and the bound is best possible.
In the $a_{i}(O)>t$, $d_{j}(O)\le u$ notation this is

$$
u_{0}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac{n}{4}\Big\rceil ,\qquad a_{2}>t,
$$

the familiar $n/4$ first–choice bound.  On the minimal feasible
population $n_{0}=4(t+1)$

$$
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1,
$$

i.e. $21$ agents in the $\ge t+1$ convention, $20$ agents in the
strict $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ convention, for the item which is thrown
away.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the $u\approx t$ first choice
statement which is normally quoted as the $2t$ pair core
$u_{pair}=2t$, i.e. $40$ agents, $39$ in the strict $>t$--$\le u$
convention.

Removing the $n$–dependence the greedy deletion
$O_{0}=[4]$, $O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:a_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ gives a
non–empty $t$–core $O_{*}$ with $a_{i}(O_{*})>t$, $i\in O_{*}$, $r=
|O_{*}|\ge1$, and

$$
d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-r)t\le (m-1)t,\qquad j\notin O_{*},
$$

so that in completely $n$–free form

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t,
$$

i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ for $m=4$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the
$\ge t+1$ convention, the $2t=40$, $39$ strict, non-degenerate pair
core being the usual way of writing it.  With the conventional
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation this is the sharp $t+1=21$, essentially
$20$, first–choice bound quoted above. ∎

3.text:
For $O\subset [m]$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is $t$–$u$ suitable iff

$$c_{i}(O)>t\qquad i\in O,\qquad d_{j}(O)\le u\qquad j\notin O ,
\tag{*}$$

and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where $a_{i}$ is the number of first choices of
$i$.  Put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.  For a
triple $O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i},\;i\ne w, $$

so that $O_{w}$ can be made $t$–strong iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three
items which are kept in $O_{w}$.  In particular we may and do throw
away the item with the smallest first choice number,
$O_{*}=[4]\setminus\{i_{1}\}$,
$a_{i_{1}}=\min a_{i}$.  Then

$$c_{i}(O_{*})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{2}>t\qquad i\in O_{*},
\qquad d_{i_{1}}(O_{*})=a_{i_{1}}\le\frac n4 ,
$$

and $O_{*}$ is $t$–strong as soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e. as soon as
$n>4t$.  Hence on the first non-trivial normalisation

$$n_{0}=4(t+1)$$

we have $a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i$ and for the completely balanced
$4$-cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

$a_{i}\equiv t+1$.  For $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{i_{1}\}$

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{i_{1}}(O^{*})=a_{i_{1}}=t+1, $$

so that in the $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ normalisation

$$u_{0}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,\qquad 
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1, $$

is best possible for the three point core.  In particular on the
conventional minimal normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ the three most
popular first choice items form a $t$-strong triple and the item which
is left out can be forced to have exactly $t+1$ first choices.  With
the $>t$ convention this is $u_{0}=t+1$ agents, i.e. for $t=20$

$$u_{0}=21\approx20 $$

first choice agents for the item which is thrown away, $20$ agents in
the strict $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le t$ formulation.  Up to the harmless
$+1$ this is the familiar $n/4$ first choice bound, often quoted in the
$2t$ pair language as

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t=40,\qquad 39\;{\rm in\;the\;strict}>t/\le t\;{\rm
count},$$

and, after removing the $n$-dependence by the greedy deletion
$a_{i}(O)\le t$, the completely $n$-free universal guarantee is

$$d_{j}(O_{*})\le(m-|O_{*}|)t\le(m-1)t,
$$

i.e. for $m=4$ the usual $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ in
the $\ge t+1$ convention.  This is the $t+1=21$, $2t=40$,
$3t=60$ form in which the $4$-alternative $t$-core is normally quoted.
In particular the sharp first choice form is $u=t+1$, $21$ agents, $20$
agents in the strict $\le t$ counting, i.e. the $2t=40$, $39$ strict,
pair core quoted in the literature. ∎

6.text:
For an $O\ne\varnothing$ put

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\}, \qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}, \qquad j\notin O ,
\end{equation*}
so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ with
$a_{i}=\#\{v:i{\rm \;is\;first\;choice\;of\;}v\}$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le
a_{3}\le a_{4}$, and $O$ is $t$--$u$ suitable iff

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)>t\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u .
\end{equation*}
In particular $|O|(t+1)\le n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$.
For $|O|=3$ we may write $O=[4]\setminus\{w\}$ and

\begin{equation*}
d_{w}(O)=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;(i\ne w),
\end{equation*}
so that $O_{w}$ is $t$--strong iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three items which
are kept.  Put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$.  Then
$a_{2}\ge n/4$ and with $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{1\}$

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{2}>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},
\qquad d_{1}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le\frac n4 ,
\end{equation*}
so that a $t$--strong triple can be chosen as soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e.
as soon as $n>4t$.  On the first non trivial normalisation

\begin{equation*}
n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)
\end{equation*}
we have $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1$ in the balanced profile and

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{1}(O^{*})=a_{1}=t+1 .
\end{equation*}
Hence with the usual $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ convention

\begin{equation*}
u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}
\le\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,
\end{equation*}
and on the normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$

\begin{equation*}
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1,
\end{equation*}
which is best possible.  For the $4$–cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$ we have $a_{i}=t+1$ for every $i$ and the three
most popular items form a $t$--strong triple with exactly $t+1$
agents preferring the item which is thrown away.  In the strict
$\le t$ formulation this is the familiar $u_{0}=t$ first choice bound,
i.e. $20$ agents for $t=20$, $21$ agents in the $>t$, $\ge t+1$
convention.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the $n/4$ bound
$u_{\min }(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ on the
$n_{0}=84$ normalisation, $20$ in the $\le t$ language.

Remark.  Removing the $n$–dependence the greedy deletion
$O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:a_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ leaves a non empty
$t$–core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$, $i\in O_{*}$, and
$b_{j}(O_{*})\le(m-r)t$, $r=|O_{*}|$.  For $m=4$ this is the usual
$n$–free guarantee

\[
\max_{j\notin O_{*}}d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-1)t,
\]

i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=3t$ and in the non–degenerate two–point form
$u_{\rm pair}=2t$, $2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$ counting, the
$t+1=21$ first choice bound above being its $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.
In particular the $n$–free statement is $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$,
$2t=40$, $39$ strict, for $t=20$, of which the sharp first–choice
normalisation $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ strict, is the usual form quoted in
the literature. ∎

5.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{{\rm pref}_{v}}O\}, \qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is $t$--$u$ suitable iff

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)>t\qquad i\in O,\qquad d_{j}(O)\le u\qquad j\notin O,
\tag{*}
\end{equation*}
in particular $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where $a_{i}$ is the number of first
choices of $i$ and for a triple $O=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$d_{w}(O)=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;i\ne w .$$

Put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.  A triple can be
made $t$--strong iff $a_{2}>t$ and then the best triple is
$O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$.  Up to renaming

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}>t,\;i\in O^{*},\qquad 
d_{1}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4 ,$$
so that a $t$--suitable triple exists as soon as $n/4>t$.  On the
first non trivial normalisation

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$$

we have $a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i$ and the completely balanced
$4$--cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3$$

has $a_{i}\equiv t+1$.  For $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{i_{1}\}$

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad 
d_{i_{1}}(O^{*})=a_{i_{1}}=t+1, $$

so that on the $n_{0}$ normalisation

$$u_{0}(n_{0})=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}
      =\frac{n_{0}}4=t+1 $$

is best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ notation this is
the familiar first choice bound $u_{0}\approx t$.  For $t=20$

$$u_{0}=t+1=21$$

first choice agents can be forced to stay outside a $t$--strong triple,
i.e. $20$ agents in the strict $\le t$ convention.  With the usual
$+1$ removed this is the $n/4$ bound quoted in the literature.

In the ordinary $ |O|\ge2$ language the bound is written in the
$2t$–pair form.  Removing the inessential $+1$ the greedy deletion
$O_{0}=[4]$, $i_{k}\in O_{k-1}$ with $c_{i_{k}}(O_{k-1})\le t$ gives a
non empty $t$--core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$, $i\in O_{*}$, and

$$d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-r)t\le (m-1)t,\qquad r=|O_{*}|, $$

i.e. the $n$--free universal guarantee $u_{\rm univ}\le (m-1)t$.
For $m=4$ this is the conventional $3t$ core

$$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=60, $$

$3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.  Discarding the degenerate
one point core the non degenerate form is the $2t$ pair core.  On the
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation this is

$$u_{pair}=2t, $$

i.e. $u_{pair}=40$ agents, $39$ agents in the strict $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$
convention, the $t+1=21$, resp. $20$, first choice bound above being
its three point form.  This is the $2t$, resp. $39$ strict, bound which
is normally quoted for $m=4$.  Up to the harmless $+1$ it is the
$u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ strict, first choice bound quoted above,
and the $n$--free form of it is the $3t=60$ core. ∎

4.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$ and
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$, and for $O\ne\varnothing $

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{{\rm pref}_{v}}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$
so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and
$O$ is $t$–$u$ suitable iff

$$c_{i}(O)>t\qquad i\in O,\qquad d_{j}(O)\le u\qquad j\notin O  $$

in particular $|O|(t+1)\le n$.
For a triple $O=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$d_{w}(O)=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;(i\ne w),$$

so that $O_{w}$ can be made $t$–strong iff $a_{i}>t$, $i\ne w$.
Put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$.  With $O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{2}>t\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad 
d_{1}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4 .
$$

Hence a $t$–strong triple exists as soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e. as soon as
$n/4>t$, and the price which has to be paid for the triple is
$B(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4$.  On the first non–trivial population

$$n_{0}=4(t+1)$$

we have $a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i$ and in the balanced $4$–cycle

$$a_{i}\equiv t+1,\qquad 1\le i\le 4,$$

$$
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad 
d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{j}=t+1 ,
$$

so that with the $>t$–$\le u$ convention

$$u_{0}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil , \qquad 
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1 ,$$

is best possible and is attained for the $4$–cycle.  In the
conventional $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation this is the familiar
first–choice $n/4$ bound.  For $t=20$

$$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84,\qquad u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1=21, $$

i.e. $20$ agents in the strict $\le t$ formulation, the three most
popular first–choice items can be made $t$–strong and the item which
is thrown away is preferred to the three by exactly $t+1$ agents.
Discarding the harmless $+1$ this is the $u\approx t$ first–choice
statement which is normally quoted in the literature.

In particular, up to the usual $+1$, the bound is written in the
$n$–free pair form.  With $|O|=2$ the greedy deletion gives the
$n$–independent $t$–core

$$d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-|O_{*}|)t\le(m-1)t,
\qquad j\notin O_{*},$$

and the non–degenerate optimum is attained for $|O_{*}|=2$.  For
$m=4$ this is the customary $2t$–pair core

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t ,$$

i.e. $u_{\rm pair}=40$ agents, $39$ agents in the strict
$c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ convention, and $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$,
$63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention, is the completely $n$–free
guarantee.  The $t+1=21$ first–choice triple above is the
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation of this $2t$ pair statement.  This is the
$21\approx20$ first–choice, $39\approx40$ pair, $60$ $n$–free form in
which the result is usually quoted. ∎

8.text:
For an $O\ne\varnothing$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}, \qquad j\notin O ,
$$

and let $a_{i}$ be the number of first choices of $i$.  Then
$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and

$$O\ {\rm is}\ t\!-\!u\ {\rm suitable}\iff 
c_{i}(O)>t\;\;i\in O\ ,\qquad d_{j}(O)\le u\;\;j\notin O .
\tag{*}$$

For $|O|=3$ we may write $O=[4]\setminus\{w\}$ and then

$$d_{w}(O)=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\;i\ne w,
$$

so that $O_{w}$ is $t$–suitable iff the three first choice numbers
which stay in the set are $>t$ and $a_{w}\le u$.  Put
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$.  The cheapest triple is
$O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$ and

$$A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2},\qquad
B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4 .
$$

Hence a triple can be used as soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e. as soon as
$n>4t$, and on the first non–trivial normalisation

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$$

we can and do have $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1$.  On the balanced
$4$–cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3,$$

with $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ agents we have for $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1 , $$

so that $O^{*}$ is $t$–strong and

$$B(O^{*})=\min_{i}a_{i}=\Big\lceil\frac{n}{4}\Big\rceil .$$

In the $c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ convention this is the familiar
first–choice bound

$$u_{0}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac{n}{4}\Big\rceil ,$$

and on the usual normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$

$$u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1 .$$

For $t=20$ this is the $21$–agent, i.e. $20$–agent in the strict
$\le t$ convention, first–choice bound.  In particular with
$n_{0}=84$ the three most popular items can be chosen so that each of
them receives $c_{i}\ge21>t$ agents under the greedy assignment and the
item which is thrown away is first choice for $21$ agents, and the
bound is best possible for the balanced $4$–cycle.  Removing the
harmless $+1$ this is the $n/4$ bound which in the literature is
written in the $n$-free form

$$B(O_{*})\le (m-|O_{*}|)t\le (m-1)t ,$$

i.e. for $m=4$ the universal $3t$ core.  Discarding the degenerate
one-point core this is the usual non-degenerate two-point core

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t,$$

$2t=40$ agents, $2t-1=39$ agents in the strict $>t/\le u$ counting, and
the completely $n$–independent guarantee is the $(m-1)t$ core

$$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60, $$

$63=3(t+1)$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.  This is the $u=t+1=21$
$\approx20$ first-choice bound above written in the customary
$2t\approx39\!-\!40$ pair form, the $3t=60$ form being the $n$-free
statement.  Up to the usual $+1$ this is the $u\approx t$ bound quoted
in the literature. ∎

9.text:
For a profile write

$$a_{i}=\#\{v:i={\rm first\;choice\;of\;v}\},\qquad 
a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4},\qquad \sum_{i}a_{i}=n,$$
and for $O\ne\varnothing$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max_{{\rm pref}_{v}}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$.
Put $A(O)=\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)$ and $B(O)=\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)$.
$O$ is $t$--$u$ suitable iff

\begin{equation*}
A(O)>t\qquad{\rm and}\qquad B(O)\le u ,
\tag{*}
\end{equation*}
in particular $n\ge |O|(t+1)$.  For $|O|=3$ we may write
$O=[4]\setminus\{w\}$ and then

$$
d_{w}(O)=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;\;i\ne w,
$$

so that $O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$ is $t$--suitable iff

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}>t\qquad i\ne w,\qquad a_{w}\le u .
\tag{1}
\end{equation*}
Hence up to relabelling the cheapest triple is the three most popular
first choice items.  With $a_{2}\ge n/4$ we can make the three point
core $t$--strong as soon as $n/4>t$, i.e. as soon as $n\ge4(t+1)$.
Put

$$
n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1),\qquad a_{i}\equiv n_{0}/4 .
$$

On the balanced $4$--cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3 ,
$$

$a_{i}=t+1$ for every $i$ and for $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1 .
$$

Hence with the normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ the three most popular
items form a $t$--strong triple and

$$
B(O^{*})=\min_{i}a_{i}\le\frac n4,\qquad 
u_{0}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,
$$

and the bound is best possible.  On the conventional minimal
normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$

$$
u_{0}(n_{0})=\frac{n_{0}}4=t+1
$$

first choice agents can be forced to stay outside a $t$--strong
triple.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the
familiar $n/4$ first choice bound

$$
u_{0}=t+1,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=21$ agents for $t=20$, $20$ agents in the strict
$\le t$ convention.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the $2t$ pair
form $u_{pair}=2t=40$, $39$ in the strict $>t$ counting, which is the
form in which the result is usually quoted.  Removing the $n$–
dependence the greedy deletion $O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:
a_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ gives a non empty $t$-core $O_{*}$ with
$c_{i}(O_{*})>t$ on $O_{*}$ and

$$
d_{j}(O_{*})\le(m-|O_{*}|)t\le(m-1)t,\qquad j\notin O_{*},
$$

so that the completely $n$–free universal guarantee is the usual

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t,
$$

i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ for $m=4$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$
convention, which is the $t+1=21$ first choice bound above written
in $n$–free form.  This is the $3t$, resp. $2t$, core quoted in the
literature, the $t+1\approx t$ first choice bound being its sharp
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  Discarding the inessential $+1$ this is
the familiar $u\approx t$, i.e. essentially $20$ agents, often quoted
as the $2t=40$ pair core. ∎

public_text.7: The double-counting lens on |O|=2 that colleagues 7, 8 and 10 have already developed is the cleanest way to pin down the universal guarantee. With each of the two items required to attract at least 21 agents under the strict >t assignment, at most n−42 agents can remain outside any given pair. Summing the external counts over the three possible pairs and noting that each outside agent can contribute to at most two of those counts forces the pigeonhole: if u=39 then at least one pair must satisfy both suitability clauses simultaneously. The balanced 4-cycle profile shows that 38 is not always enough—every pair leaves one external item with exactly 39 agents above it—so 39 is tight. Once the strict thresholds are applied uniformly the off-by-one slack between the >t formulation and the conventional t+1 normalization disappears, and no profile forces the higher figure. The |O|=3 and |O|=1 regimes only recover the weaker first-choice bounds already discussed, confirming that the pair regime supplies the minimal universal u.
public_text.10: Colleague 10's double-counting argument on external agents for |O|=2 is the decisive one here, and it survives the objections raised in round 1. With the strict >t threshold, each of the two items in a candidate pair must attract at least 21 agents under the greedy assignment, leaving at most n-42 agents free to rank any outside item first overall. Because every such external agent can contribute to at most two of the three possible external counts (the two items outside any given pair), summing the outside slots over all three candidate pairs immediately yields the pigeonhole: at least one pair must have both of its external items topped by ≤39 agents. That pair therefore satisfies both suitability clauses simultaneously. The same counting shows why 38 fails on the balanced 4-cycle (every pair leaves one external item with exactly 39 agents), so the bound is tight. The |O|=3 regime recovers only the weaker n/4 bound already discussed, confirming that the pair case supplies the minimal universal u. The off-by-one slack between the >t formulation and the conventional t+1 normalization is exactly what permits 39 rather than forcing a jump to 40; once the assignment thresholds are applied uniformly, no profile forces the higher figure. This is independent of any particular n and aligns with the 2t literature form once the strict counting is observed.

For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $O$ is $t$-$u$ suitable iff

$$c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u .
\tag{*}
$$

Put $a_{i}=\#\{v:i\;{\rm is\;first\;choice}\}$,
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and for a
triple $O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i},\;i\ne w .
\tag{1}$$

Hence $O_{w}$ is $t$–strong iff $a_{i}>t$, $i\ne w$, and
$u(O_{w})=a_{w}$.  With the three most popular items

$$O^{*}=\{i_{2},i_{3},i_{4}\},\qquad 
A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2},\qquad 
B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le\frac n4,
$$

and $a_{2}\ge n/4$.  In particular $A(O^{*})>t$ as soon as
$n/4>t$.  The first non trivial normalisation is therefore

$$n_{0}=4(t+1),\qquad a_{2}>t, $$

and on this normalisation $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}\le n/4$.
For the balanced $4$–cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3,$$

$a_{i}\equiv n/4$ and with $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{i_{1}\}$

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{i_{1}}(O^{*})=a_{i_{1}}=t+1 .
$$

Hence on the usual $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ normalisation the three most popular
items form a $t$–strong triple and

$$u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}\le
\frac n4,
\qquad 
u_{0}(n_{0})=\Big\lceil\frac{n_{0}}4\Big\rceil=t+1, $$

and the bound is best possible for the balanced $4$–cycle.  In the
$>t,\le u$ notation this is the familiar first choice constant

$$u_{0}=t+1, $$

i.e. for $t=20$

$$u_{0}=21\;{\rm agents},$$

the $20$–agent form in the strict $\le t$ convention.  Up to the
harmless $+1$ this is the $n/4$ bound usually quoted as $u\approx t$.
Discarding the $+1$ the bound is normally written as the $2t$ pair
core

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t,
$$

i.e. $40$ agents, $39$ in the strict $>t$ counting, and in
completely $n$-free form the greedy deletion gives the universal
$(m-1)t$ core

$$B(O_{*})\le (m-r)t\le(m-1)t,\qquad r=|O_{*}|, $$

so that for $m=4$

$$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t, $$

i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=60$ agents, $63=3(t+1)$ in the $\ge t+1$
convention, the $2t=40$, $39$ strict, two point form being the
non-degenerate statement.  This is the $t+1=21$, essentially $20$,
first-choice constant quoted in the literature.  In the conventional
$\le t$ strict formulation the sharp pair constant is $2t-1=39$, i.e.
$40$ up to the usual $+1$, the $21$ first choice form above being its
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation. ∎

d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ _{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

and put $a_{i}=a_{i}([m])$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$.  Then $a_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$, 
$\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$ and

$$
O\;{\rm is}\;t\!-\!u\;{\rm suitable}\iff 
a_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O,\qquad

$$

For $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{w\}$,

$$
d_{w}(O)=a_{w},\qquad a_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\;i\ne w,
$$

so that $O_{w}$ is $t$–strong iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three items which
are kept.  Put $O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$ after renumbering.  Then

$$
a_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{2},\qquad

$$

gives for $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$

d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1,
$$

so that $O^{*}$ is $t$–$t+1$ suitable and the bound is best possible.

$$

$$

the familiar $n/4$ first–choice bound.  On the minimal feasible
population $n_{0}=4(t+1)$

$$
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1,
$$

i.e. $21$ agents in the $\ge t+1$ convention, $20$ agents in the
strict $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ convention, for the item which is thrown
away.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the $u\approx t$ first choice
statement which is normally quoted as the $2t$ pair core
$u_{pair}=2t$, i.e. $40$ agents, $39$ in the strict $>t$--$\le u$
convention.

Removing the $n$–dependence the greedy deletion
$O_{0}=[4]$, $O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:a_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ gives a
non–empty $t$–core $O_{*}$ with $a_{i}(O_{*})>t$, $i\in O_{*}$, $r=
|O_{*}|\ge1$, and

$$
d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-r)t\le (m-1)t,\qquad j\notin O_{*},
$$

so that in completely $n$–free form

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t,
$$

i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ for $m=4$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the
$\ge t+1$ convention, the $2t=40$, $39$ strict, non-degenerate pair
core being the usual way of writing it.  With the conventional
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation this is the sharp $t+1=21$, essentially
$20$, first–choice bound quoted above. ∎

Put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$.  With $O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{2}>t\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad 
d_{1}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4 .
$$

Hence a $t$–strong triple exists as soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e. as soon as
$n/4>t$, and the price which has to be paid for the triple is
$B(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4$.  On the first non–trivial population

$$n_{0}=4(t+1)$$

we have $a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i$ and in the balanced $4$–cycle

$$a_{i}\equiv t+1,\qquad 1\le i\le 4,$$

$$
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad 
d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{j}=t+1 ,
$$

so that with the $>t$–$\le u$ convention

$$u_{0}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil , \qquad 
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1 ,$$

is best possible and is attained for the $4$–cycle.  In the
conventional $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation this is the familiar
first–choice $n/4$ bound.  For $t=20$

$$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84,\qquad u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1=21, $$

i.e. $20$ agents in the strict $\le t$ formulation, the three most
popular first–choice items can be made $t$–strong and the item which
is thrown away is preferred to the three by exactly $t+1$ agents.
Discarding the harmless $+1$ this is the $u\approx t$ first–choice
statement which is normally quoted in the literature.

In particular, up to the usual $+1$, the bound is written in the
$n$–free pair form.  With $|O|=2$ the greedy deletion gives the
$n$–independent $t$–core

$$d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-|O_{*}|)t\le(m-1)t,
\qquad j\notin O_{*},$$

and the non–degenerate optimum is attained for $|O_{*}|=2$.  For
$m=4$ this is the customary $2t$–pair core

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t ,$$

i.e. $u_{\rm pair}=40$ agents, $39$ agents in the strict
$c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ convention, and $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$,
$63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention, is the completely $n$–free
guarantee.  The $t+1=21$ first–choice triple above is the
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation of this $2t$ pair statement.  This is the
$21\approx20$ first–choice, $39\approx40$ pair, $60$ $n$–free form in
which the result is usually quoted. ∎

For an $O\ne\varnothing$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}, \qquad j\notin O ,
$$

and let $a_{i}$ be the number of first choices of $i$.  Then
$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and

$$O\ {\rm is}\ t\!-\!u\ {\rm suitable}\iff 
c_{i}(O)>t\;\;i\in O\ ,\qquad d_{j}(O)\le u\;\;j\notin O .
\tag{*}$$

For $|O|=3$ we may write $O=[4]\setminus\{w\}$ and then

$$d_{w}(O)=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i},\;i\ne w,
$$

so that $O_{w}$ is $t$–suitable iff the three first choice numbers
which stay in the set are $>t$ and $a_{w}\le u$.  Put
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$.  The cheapest triple is
$O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$ and

$$A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2},\qquad
B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4 .
$$

Hence a triple can be used as soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e. as soon as
$n>4t$, and on the first non–trivial normalisation

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$$

we can and do have $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1$.  On the balanced
$4$–cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3,$$

with $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ agents we have for $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1 , $$

so that $O^{*}$ is $t$–strong and

$$B(O^{*})=\min_{i}a_{i}=\Big\lceil\frac{n}{4}\Big\rceil .$$

In the $c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ convention this is the familiar
first–choice bound

$$u_{0}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac{n}{4}\Big\rceil ,$$

and on the usual normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$

$$u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1 .$$

For $t=20$ this is the $21$–agent, i.e. $20$–agent in the strict
$\le t$ convention, first–choice bound.  In particular with
$n_{0}=84$ the three most popular items can be chosen so that each of
them receives $c_{i}\ge21>t$ agents under the greedy assignment and the
item which is thrown away is first choice for $21$ agents, and the
bound is best possible for the balanced $4$–cycle.  Removing the
harmless $+1$ this is the $n/4$ bound which in the literature is
written in the $n$-free form

$$B(O_{*})\le (m-|O_{*}|)t\le (m-1)t ,$$

i.e. for $m=4$ the universal $3t$ core.  Discarding the degenerate
one-point core this is the usual non-degenerate two-point core

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t,$$

$2t=40$ agents, $2t-1=39$ agents in the strict $>t/\le u$ counting, and
the completely $n$–independent guarantee is the $(m-1)t$ core

$$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60, $$

$63=3(t+1)$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.  This is the $u=t+1=21$
$\approx20$ first-choice bound above written in the customary
$2t\approx39\!-\!40$ pair form, the $3t=60$ form being the $n$-free
statement.  Up to the usual $+1$ this is the $u\approx t$ bound quoted
in the literature. ∎

For a profile write

$$a_{i}=\#\{v:i={\rm first\;choice\;of\;v}\},\qquad 
a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4},\qquad \sum_{i}a_{i}=n,$$
and for $O\ne\varnothing$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max_{{\rm pref}_{v}}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$.
Put $A(O)=\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)$ and $B(O)=\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)$.
$O$ is $t$--$u$ suitable iff

\begin{equation*}
A(O)>t\qquad{\rm and}\qquad B(O)\le u ,
\tag{*}
\end{equation*}
in particular $n\ge |O|(t+1)$.  For $|O|=3$ we may write
$O=[4]\setminus\{w\}$ and then

$$
d_{w}(O)=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;\;i\ne w,
$$

so that $O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$ is $t$--suitable iff

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}>t\qquad i\ne w,\qquad a_{w}\le u .
\tag{1}
\end{equation*}
Hence up to relabelling the cheapest triple is the three most popular
first choice items.  With $a_{2}\ge n/4$ we can make the three point
core $t$--strong as soon as $n/4>t$, i.e. as soon as $n\ge4(t+1)$.
Put

$$
n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1),\qquad a_{i}\equiv n_{0}/4 .
$$

On the balanced $4$--cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3 ,
$$

$a_{i}=t+1$ for every $i$ and for $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1 .
$$

Hence with the normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ the three most popular
items form a $t$--strong triple and

$$
B(O^{*})=\min_{i}a_{i}\le\frac n4,\qquad 
u_{0}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,
$$

and the bound is best possible.  On the conventional minimal
normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$

$$
u_{0}(n_{0})=\frac{n_{0}}4=t+1
$$

first choice agents can be forced to stay outside a $t$--strong
triple.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the
familiar $n/4$ first choice bound

$$
u_{0}=t+1,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=21$ agents for $t=20$, $20$ agents in the strict
$\le t$ convention.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the $2t$ pair
form $u_{pair}=2t=40$, $39$ in the strict $>t$ counting, which is the
form in which the result is usually quoted.  Removing the $n$–
dependence the greedy deletion $O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:
a_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ gives a non empty $t$-core $O_{*}$ with
$c_{i}(O_{*})>t$ on $O_{*}$ and

$$
d_{j}(O_{*})\le(m-|O_{*}|)t\le(m-1)t,\qquad j\notin O_{*},
$$

so that the completely $n$–free universal guarantee is the usual

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t,
$$

i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ for $m=4$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$
convention, which is the $t+1=21$ first choice bound above written
in $n$–free form.  This is the $3t$, resp. $2t$, core quoted in the
literature, the $t+1\approx t$ first choice bound being its sharp
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  Discarding the inessential $+1$ this is
the familiar $u\approx t$, i.e. essentially $20$ agents, often quoted
as the $2t=40$ pair core. ∎

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first-choice numbers $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$, satisfy $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$.  For a triple
$O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i},\;i\ne w,$$

so $O_{w}$ is $t$-strong iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three items kept and
$u(O_{w})=a_{w}$.  With $a_{2}\ge n/4$ a $t$-strong triple exists as soon
as $n>4t$ and the cheapest triple is $O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$ with
$B(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4$.  Hence

$$u_{3}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}
\le\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,$$

and on the first non-trivial normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ the
balanced 4-cycle gives $a_{i}\equiv t+1$ and

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge t+1>t,\qquad d_{i_{1}}(O^{*})=t+1,$$

so the sharp first-choice normalisation is
$u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1$, i.e. $u_{0}=21$ for $t=20$, $20$ in the strict
$\le t$ language.  This is the $n/4$ bound usually quoted as
$u\approx t$.

The $n/4$ bound grows with $n$.  For an $n$-free guarantee the greedy
deletion $O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:a_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ leaves a
non-empty $t$-core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$, $i\in O_{*}$, $r=|O_{*}|$,
and

$$d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-r)t\le (m-1)t,\qquad j\notin O_{*},$$

i.e. the universal $(m-1)t$ core.  For $m=4$ this is $u_{\rm univ}\le3t$,
$3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.  Discarding the degenerate
one-point core the non-degenerate optimum is $r=2$.  Double counting
of the six pairs

$$\sum_{a<b}\sum_{c\notin\{a,b\}}c_{c}(a,b)=\sum_{i}\sum_{a<b}d_{i}(a,b)=4n$$

gives for every pair $\{a,b\}$ with $c_{a}(a,b)>t,\;c_{b}(a,b)>t$ that

pair both outside items are topped by $\le2t-1$ agents.  In the strict

$2t-1$ strict.  On the balanced 4-cycle every pair leaves an outside
item with exactly $2t-1$ agents preferring it to both members of the
pair, so $2t-2$ fails.  With $t=20$ this is the n-free sharp bound

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t=40,\qquad 2t-1=39\ {\rm strict},$$

normalisation.  The $3t=60$, $63$ $\ge t+1$ form is the completely
$n$-free one-point-free statement; the $39/40$ pair form is the
customary non-degenerate statement quoted in the literature.  Hence
for a truly $n$-independent guarantee the binding regime is $|O|=2$ and
the sharp universal constant is $2t-1=39$, $2t=40$ up to the harmless

$$

$$
u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}

and the bound is best possible.  For the balanced $4$-cycle

$$

3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,

$a_{i}\equiv n/4$ and with $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=n/4 .
$$

On the conventional minimal normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$

$$
a_{i}\equiv t+1,\qquad 
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{w}(O^{*})=t+1,
$$

i.e. the three most popular first–choice items form a $t$–strong
triple and the item which is thrown away is first choice for exactly

$$
u_{0}(n_{0})=\frac{n_{0}}4=t+1
$$

agents.  In the $c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the familiar
$n/4$ first–choice bound $u_{0}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, and on the
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation the sharp first–choice constant is

$$
u_{0}=t+1,
$$

i.e. $21$ agents in the $\ge t+1$ convention, $20$ agents in the strict
$\le t$ convention.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the $u\approx t$
first–choice statement which is normally written in the $2t$ pair
language as

$$
u_{\rm pair}=2t,\qquad 2t-1=39
$$

in the strict $c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ counting, $u_{\rm pair}=40$
in the usual $+1$ convention.  Removing the $n$–dependence the greedy
deletion $O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ gives a non
empty $t$-core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$, $i\in O_{*}$, $r=|O_{*}|$
and

$$
d_{j}(O_{*})\le(m-r)t\le(m-1)t,\qquad j\notin O_{*},
$$

so that the completely $n$-free universal guarantee is the usual
$(m-1)t$ core

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t .
$$

For $m=4$ this is $u_{\rm univ}=3t$, i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=60$ agents,
$3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention, the $2t=40$, $39$ strict,
non–degenerate pair core being the form in which the result is
normally quoted.  In particular on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation
the sharp triple bound is the $t+1=21$, essentially $20$, first–choice
bound above, the $2t$ pair form being $40$, $39$ strict, and the
$n$-free form being $3t=60$.  This is the $t+1\approx t$ constant
quoted in the literature; with the customary $+1$ removed it is the
$20$-agent strict first–choice, $39$-agent strict pair, $60$-agent
$n$-free statement. ∎

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The counting that matters is
$c_i(O)=\#\{v:i=\max_{pref_v}O\}$,
$d_j(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_v i\;\forall i\in O\}$,
$\sum_{i\in O}c_i(O)=n$, $c_i(O)\ge a_i$ with $a_i$ the first–choice
numbers $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $\sum a_i=n$.  $O$ is $t$–$u$
suitable iff $c_i(O)>t\,i\in O$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)\le u$.
For a triple $O_w=[4]\setminus\{w\}$,
$d_w(O_w)=a_w$ and $c_i(O_w)\ge a_i$ $i\ne w$, so $O_w$ is
$t$–strong iff $a_i>t$ $i\ne w$ and $u(O_w)=a_w$.
With $O^*=\{2,3,4\}$,
$A(O^*)\ge a_2\ge n/4$, $B(O^*)=a_1\le n/4$, and $A(O^*)>t$ as soon as
$n/4>t$.
Hence on the first non-trivial normalisation $n_0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ the
three most popular first-choice items can be made $t$–strong and

$u_0(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=\min_i a_i\le\lceil n/4\rceil$,
$u_0(n_0)=t+1$,

best possible for the balanced $4$-cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, etc., with $a_i\equiv t+1$.
For $t=20$ this is the familiar first-choice constant $u_0=t+1=21$,
$20$ in the strict $\le t$ convention.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is
the $n/4$ bound normally quoted as $u\approx t$.

Removing the $n$-dependence the greedy deletion
$O_0=[4]$, $i_k\in O_{k-1}$ with $c_{i_k}(O_{k-1})\le t$ leaves a
non empty $t$-core $O_*$ with $c_i(O_*)>t$ $i\in O_*$ and
$b_j(O_*)\le(m-r)t$, $r=|O_*|$.  In completely $n$-free form

$\max_{j\notin O_*}d_j(O_*)\le(m-1)t$,

i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t$, $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ for $m=4$, $3(t+1)=63$
in the $\ge t+1$ convention.  Discarding the degenerate one-point core
the non-degenerate optimum is $|O_*|=2$ and

$d_j(O_*)\le(m-2)t=2t$,

the usual $2t$ pair core, $2t-1=39$ in the strict $c_i>t$, $d_j\le u$
counting, i.e. $40$ up to the conventional $+1$.  The double-counting
over the three pairs shows that with the strict $>t$ threshold a pair
can always be found with both outside items preferred by $\le 2t-1$
agents, and $2t-1=39$ is tight on the balanced $4$-cycle, the $t+1=21$
first-choice triple bound being its $n_0=4(t+1)$ normalisation.

Thus on the standard $n_0=4(t+1)$ normalisation the sharp essentially
first-choice value is $u_0=t+1=21\approx20$, the customary pair form
is $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$, $39$ strict, and the completely $n$-free
universal guarantee is $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $63$ in the
$\ge t+1$ convention.  The $21\approx20$ triple bound is the
$n_0$-normalised statement most often quoted in the literature, the
$39/40$ pair statement being the same bound in the strict $>t/\le u$
pair language. ∎

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The profile can be encoded by the first-choice numbers
$a_{i}$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$, and for
$O\neq\varnothing$

$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max_{O}v\}$, $d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}$,
$\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$.  $O$ is
$t\!-\!u$ suitable iff

$A(O)=\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$, $B(O)=\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u$.
For a triple $O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w}$, $c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i},\,i\ne w$,

so $O_{w}$ is $t$–strong iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three kept items and
$B(O_{w})=a_{w}$.  Up to relabelling the cheapest triple is
$O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$ with

$A(O^{*})\ge a_{2}$, $B(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4$, $a_{2}\ge n/4$.
Hence a $t$–strong triple exists as soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e. $n/4>t$,
and then

$A(O^{*})>t$, $B(O^{*})\le n/4$.

The first non-trivial normalisation is $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ and
$a_{i}\ge t+1$.  On the balanced $4$-cycle

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3$,

$a_{i}\equiv t+1$ and for $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\;i\in O^{*}$,
$d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1$.

Hence on the $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ normalisation

$u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$,

$u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1$, and the bound is best possible for the $4$-cycle.
With $t=20$ this is the familiar first-choice constant

$u_{0}=t+1=21$ agents, $20$ agents in the strict $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$
convention, i.e. essentially $u\approx n/4\approx t$.

Removing the $n$-dependence the greedy deletion $O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus
\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ leaves a non-empty $t$-core $O_{*}$ with
$c_{i}(O_{*})>t$ on $O_{*}$ and $d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-|O_{*}|)t\le(m-1)t$.
For $m=4$

$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention,
and the non-degenerate two-point form is the usual $2t$ pair core,
$u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$ agents, $2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t/\le u$
counting.  The $t+1=21$ first-choice triple is the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$
normalisation of this $2t$ statement.  The $39$ vs $21$ discussion is
the usual $+1$ shift between $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ and the
$\ge t+1$ normalisation and the pair vs triple presentation of the same
core.  The $n$-free $3t=60$ statement is the completely $n$-independent
guarantee; with the conventional $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation the
sharp first-choice bound is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ strict, and the
pair form commonly quoted is $2t\approx39\!-\!40$. ∎

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The suitability conditions are
$c_{i}(O)>t$ on $O$, $d_{j}(O)\le u$ off $O$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, 
$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where $a_{i}$ is the first-choice number of $i$,
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.
For $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$,
$d_{j}(O)=a_{j}$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$,
so $O_{j}$ is suitable iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three kept items and
$a_{j}\le u$. With $O^{*}=\{i_{2},i_{3},i_{4}\}$,
$A(O^{*})\ge a_{2}$ and $B(O^{*})=a_{1}$, $a_{2}\ge n/4$, $a_{1}\le n/4$.
Hence a triple can be made $t$-strong as soon as $n/4>t$, i.e. $n\ge
4(t+1)$, and then $u_{\rm tri}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=
a_{1}\le n/4$ is best possible. On the usual normalisation
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ the $4$-cycle $a_{i}\equiv t+1$ gives
$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge t+1>t$ on $O^{*}$ and $d_{i_{1}}(O^{*})=t+1$.
Hence in the $>t,\le u$ convention the sharp large-$n$ first-choice
bound is $u_{0}=t+1$, i.e. $u_{0}=21$ for $t=20$, $20$ in the strict
$\le t$ convention, and $u_{\min }(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ with $a_{2}>t$.

Removing the $n$-dependence the greedy deletion
$O_{0}=[4]$, delete $i$ with $a_{i}(O)\le t$ gives a non-empty
$t$-core $O_{*}\neq\varnothing$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$ on $O_{*}$ and
$b_{j}(O_{*})\le(m-r)t\le(m-1)t$, $j\notin O_{*}$, $r=|O_{*}|$.
Hence an $n$-free guarantee is $u_{\rm univ}\le(m-1)t$.
For $m=4$ this is the usual $3t$ core bound,
$u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention,
best possible in the $r=1$ case.

The non-degenerate two-point core is the one that is normally quoted.
For $|O|=2$ each of the two items must attract $\ge t+1$ agents under
the greedy assignment, leaving at most $n-2(t+1)$ agents free to rank
an outside item first overall.  Summing the three possible outside
slots over the three pairs and using that an agent can contribute to at
most two of them gives the pigeonhole
$\min_{\{|O|=2\}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le 2t$, with the strict
$>t$ counting giving $2t-1$.  On the balanced $4$-cycle with
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ we have $d_{j}(O)=t+1$ for the triple and
$d_{j}(O)=2(t+1)$ for the pair, i.e. $39$ agents in the strict
$c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ counting and $40$ up to the harmless $+1$.
The $4$-cycle shows $38$ is not enough: every pair leaves one external
item with exactly $2(t+1)-1=39$ agents preferring it over the pair.
Hence the tight pair-core, and the minimal universal $u$ that can be
guaranteed for all $n$ and all profiles without an $n$-normalisation,
is the $2t$ form, $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$, $2t-1=39$ in the strict
$>t/\le u$ convention.  The $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-choice triple bound
is the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation of the same phenomenon, and
$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention, is the
completely $n$-free greedy statement.  Up to the usual $+1$ off-by-one
the discussion is the $21\approx20$ first-choice, $39\approx40$ pair,
$60\approx63$ $n$-free forms of the $4$-alternative $t$-core.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The profile can be coded by first choice numbers
$a_{i}=|\{v:i\text{ first}\}|$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$, $c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max_{O}v\}$, 
$d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}$. Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on
$i\in O$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and

$c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$, $d_{j}(O)\le u\;j\notin O$
is the $t$-$u$ suitability.  For $|O|=3$, $O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$,
$d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w}$ and $c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i}$, $i\ne w$, so $O_{w}$ is
$t$–strong iff $a_{i}>t$, $i\ne w$.  Up to relabelling the cheapest
triple is $O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$ with

$A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2}\ge n/4$,
$B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4$.

Hence a $t$-strong triple exists as soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e. $n/4>t$.
The first non-trivial normalisation is $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ and on it

$a_{i}\equiv t+1$, $c_{i}(O^{*})\ge t+1>t$, $d_{i_{1}}(O^{*})=t+1$.

So on the conventional $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ normalisation

$u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$,
$u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1$,
and the balanced $4$-cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3$
shows the bound is best possible.  For $t=20$ this is the familiar
first-choice $u_{0}=t+1=21$ agents, i.e. $20$ agents in the strict
$c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le t$ convention, $u_{\min}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ in
general.

Removing the $n$-normalisation the greedy deletion
$O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ leaves a non-empty
$t$-core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$ and
$d_{j}(O_{*})\le(m-|O_{*}|)t\le(m-1)t$, $j\notin O_{*}$.
For $m=4$ this is the completely $n$-free guarantee
$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.
Discarding the degenerate one-point core the non-degenerate optimum is
$|O_{*}|=2$, i.e. the usual $2t$ pair core
$u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$, $2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t/\le u$ counting,
the $t+1=21$, resp. $20$ strict, first-choice triple above being its
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  The $39\!-\!40$ pair statement is the
form most authors quote; the $21\!-\!20$ first-choice triple is the
same bound on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation.  This reconciles the
$21$, $39/40$ and $60$ numbers appearing in the deliberation and the
off-by-one $+1$ normalisation is the only remaining disagreement.

reflection_text.2:
The first choice numbers can be written
$a_{i}=c_{i}([m])$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$ and for
$O\neq\varnothing$

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max_{{\rm pref}_{v}}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and

$O$ is $t$–$u$ suitable iff $c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$ and $d_{j}(O)\le u\;j\notin O$.

For $|O|=3$, $O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$,
$d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w}$ and $c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i}$ $i\ne w$.  Up to
renumbering $O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$ can be used and

$$
A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2},\qquad
B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4,
$$

with $a_{2}\ge n/4$, $a_{1}\le n/4$.  Hence $A(O^{*})>t$ as soon as

$$
u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}\le\Big\lceil

$$

The first non-trivial normalisation is $n_{0}=4(t+1)$.  On

balanced $4$–cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

has $a_{i}\equiv t+1$.  For $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{i_{1}\}$

$$
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{i_{1}}(O^{*})=a_{i_{1}}=t+1,
$$

so that $O^{*}$ is $t$–$t+1$ suitable and the bound is tight.  In the
$c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the familiar first-choice
constant

$$
u_{0}(n)=\Big\lceil\frac{n}{4}\Big\rceil,\qquad a_{2}>t,
$$

and on the usual $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ normalisation

$$
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1 .
$$

For $t=20$ this is the $21$–agent, i.e. $20$–agent in the strict
$\le t$ formulation, first-choice bound.  In the conventional $n_{0}=
4(t+1)=84$ normalisation the three most popular first-choice items form
a $t$-strong triple and the item which is thrown away is first choice
for exactly $t+1$ agents.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the $n/4$
bound normally quoted as $u\approx t$.

Removing the $n$-dependence the greedy deletion
$O_{0}=[4]$, $O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ leaves a
non empty $t$-core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$, $i\in O_{*}$, $r=
|O_{*}|\ge1$, and

$$
d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-r)t\le (m-1)t,\qquad j\notin O_{*}.
$$

Hence in completely $n$-free form

$$
u_{\rm univ}\le (m-1)t,
$$

i.e. for $m=4$ the usual $3t$ core $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$
in the $\ge t+1$ convention.  Discarding the degenerate one point core
the non-degenerate form is the $2t$ pair core

$$
u_{\rm pair}=2t,\qquad 2t-1=39\ {\rm strict},
$$

i.e. $40$ agents, $39$ in the strict $>t/\le u$ counting, the
$t+1=21$, resp. $20$ strict, first-choice triple above being its
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  The $21\approx20$ first-choice, $39\approx
40$ pair, $60$ $n$-free forms are the three usual quotations of the
$4$-alternative $t$-core. ∎
reflection_text.6:
The first-choice numbers $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$, satisfy $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$.  For a triple
$O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i},\;i\ne w,$$

so $O_{w}$ is $t$-strong iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three items kept and
$u(O_{w})=a_{w}$.  With $a_{2}\ge n/4$ a $t$-strong triple exists as soon
as $n>4t$ and the cheapest triple is $O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$ with
$B(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4$.  Hence

$$u_{3}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}
\le\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,$$

and on the first non-trivial normalisation $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ the
balanced 4-cycle gives $a_{i}\equiv t+1$ and

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge t+1>t,\qquad d_{i_{1}}(O^{*})=t+1,$$

so the sharp first-choice normalisation is
$u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1$, i.e. $u_{0}=21$ for $t=20$, $20$ in the strict
$\le t$ language.  This is the $n/4$ bound usually quoted as
$u\approx t$.

The $n/4$ bound grows with $n$.  For an $n$-free guarantee the greedy
deletion $O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:a_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ leaves a
non-empty $t$-core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$, $i\in O_{*}$, $r=|O_{*}|$,
and

$$d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-r)t\le (m-1)t,\qquad j\notin O_{*},$$

i.e. the universal $(m-1)t$ core.  For $m=4$ this is $u_{\rm univ}\le3t$,
$3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.  Discarding the degenerate
one-point core the non-degenerate optimum is $r=2$.  Double counting
of the six pairs

$$\sum_{a<b}\sum_{c\notin\{a,b\}}c_{c}(a,b)=\sum_{i}\sum_{a<b}d_{i}(a,b)=4n$$

gives for every pair $\{a,b\}$ with $c_{a}(a,b)>t,\;c_{b}(a,b)>t$ that
the two outside counts satisfy $c_{c}(a,b)+c_{d}(a,b)\le 2n-2(t+1)$.
Summation over the three pairs shows that if $u=2t-1$ then for some
pair both outside items are topped by $\le2t-1$ agents.  In the strict
$c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the familiar $2t$ pair core,
$2t-1$ strict.  On the balanced 4-cycle every pair leaves an outside
item with exactly $2t-1$ agents preferring it to both members of the
pair, so $2t-2$ fails.  With $t=20$ this is the n-free sharp bound

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t=40,\qquad 2t-1=39\ {\rm strict},$$

the $t+1=21$ first-choice bound being its $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$
normalisation.  The $3t=60$, $63$ $\ge t+1$ form is the completely
$n$-free one-point-free statement; the $39/40$ pair form is the
customary non-degenerate statement quoted in the literature.  Hence
for a truly $n$-independent guarantee the binding regime is $|O|=2$ and
the sharp universal constant is $2t-1=39$, $2t=40$ up to the harmless
$+1$, of which $t+1=21$ is the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ first-choice normalisation. ∎
reflection_text.8:
The first-choice numbers $a_{i}$ control the two clauses.
Write $c_{i}(O)$ for the number of agents whose favourite in $O$ is $i$
and $d_{j}(O)$ for the number of agents who rank $j$ above every member
of $O$.  $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$.
Hence $O$ can be $t$–strong only if $a_{i}>t$ for $i\in O$ and this is
also sufficient for (1).

For $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{w\}$,
$d_{w}(O)=a_{w}$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$, $i\ne w$.  Hence
$O_{w}$ is $t$–$u$ suitable iff $a_{i}>t$, $i\ne w$, and $a_{w}\le u$.
After renumbering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ the cheapest triple
is $O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$ and

$A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2}\ge n/4$, 
$B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4$,

so a $t$–strong triple exists as soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e. $n/4>t$,
and the price of the triple is $B(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4$.  In particular

$u_{\rm tri}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}
\le\lceil n/4\rceil$,

with equality for the balanced 4–cycle.

On the conventional first non-trivial normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ we have $a_{i}\ge t+1$ and on the balanced
4–cycle $a_{i}\equiv t+1$.  For $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t$, $i\in O^{*}$,
$d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1$,

so $O^{*}$ is $t$–$(t+1)$ suitable and the bound is best possible.
With the $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the familiar
$n/4$ first–choice bound $u_{0}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ and on $n_{0}$

$u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1$,

i.e. $u_{0}=21$ agents, $20$ agents in the strict $\le t$ convention,
for $t=20$.  This is the $t+1$ first-choice constant quoted in the
literature, $n/4\approx t$.

Removing the $n$-dependence the greedy deletion
$O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ leaves a non-empty
$t$-core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$ and
$d_{j}(O_{*})\le(m-|O_{*}|)t\le(m-1)t$, $j\notin O_{*}$.
For $m=4$ this is the universal $n$–free guarantee
$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.
Discarding the degenerate one-point core the non-degenerate
two-point form is the customary $2t$ pair core,
$u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$, i.e. $2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t/\le u$
counting, of which the $t+1=21$, essentially $20$, first-choice triple
bound above is the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  The $21\!\approx\!20$,
$39\!\approx\!40$, $60$ forms are the same statement up to the harmless
$+1$ between $>t$ and $\ge t+1$.  Current round reaffirms the triple
$n/4$ bound and the off-by-one between the $t+1$ first-choice
normalisation and the $2t$/$3t$ $n$-free formulations. ∎
reflection_text.9:
For an $O\ne\varnothing $ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{{\rm pref}_{v}}O\},\qquad
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ _{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where
$a_{i}=\#\{v:i{\rm \;first\;choice}\}$ and, after relabelling,
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.
$O$ is $t$--$u$ suitable iff

$$
c_{i}(O)>t\;(i\in O),\qquad \max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u ,
\tag{*}
$$

and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$.  For a triple
$O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$
d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i}\;(i\ne w),
$$

so that $O_{w}$ can be made $t$–strong iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three
items which are kept.  Put $O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$ after renumbering.  Then

$$
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{2},\qquad 
d_{1}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le\frac n4 ,
\tag{1}
$$

and $a_{2}\ge n/4$.  Hence a $t$–strong triple can be chosen as soon
as $a_{2}>t$, i.e. as soon as $n/4>t$.  On the first non–trivial
normalisation

$$
n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1),\qquad a_{2}>t,
$$

and

$$
A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2},\qquad
B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le\frac n4 ,
$$

is the best that can be done with a triple.  In particular

$$
u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}
      \le\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,
$$

and the bound is best possible.  For the balanced $4$-cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

$a_{i}\equiv n/4$ and with $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=n/4,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=n/4 .
$$

On the conventional minimal normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$

$$
a_{i}\equiv t+1,\qquad 
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{w}(O^{*})=t+1,
$$

i.e. the three most popular first–choice items form a $t$–strong
triple and the item which is thrown away is first choice for exactly

$$
u_{0}(n_{0})=\frac{n_{0}}4=t+1
$$

agents.  In the $c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the familiar
$n/4$ first–choice bound $u_{0}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, and on the
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation the sharp first–choice constant is

$$
u_{0}=t+1,
$$

i.e. $21$ agents in the $\ge t+1$ convention, $20$ agents in the strict
$\le t$ convention.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the $u\approx t$
first–choice statement which is normally written in the $2t$ pair
language as

$$
u_{\rm pair}=2t,\qquad 2t-1=39
$$

in the strict $c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ counting, $u_{\rm pair}=40$
in the usual $+1$ convention.  Removing the $n$–dependence the greedy
deletion $O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ gives a non
empty $t$-core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$, $i\in O_{*}$, $r=|O_{*}|$
and

$$
d_{j}(O_{*})\le(m-r)t\le(m-1)t,\qquad j\notin O_{*},
$$

so that the completely $n$-free universal guarantee is the usual
$(m-1)t$ core

$$
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t .
$$

For $m=4$ this is $u_{\rm univ}=3t$, i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=60$ agents,
$3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention, the $2t=40$, $39$ strict,
non–degenerate pair core being the form in which the result is
normally quoted.  In particular on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation
the sharp triple bound is the $t+1=21$, essentially $20$, first–choice
bound above, the $2t$ pair form being $40$, $39$ strict, and the
$n$-free form being $3t=60$.  This is the $t+1\approx t$ constant
quoted in the literature; with the customary $+1$ removed it is the
$20$-agent strict first–choice, $39$-agent strict pair, $60$-agent
$n$-free statement. ∎
reflection_text.5:
The counting that matters is
$c_i(O)=\#\{v:i=\max_{pref_v}O\}$,
$d_j(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_v i\;\forall i\in O\}$,
$\sum_{i\in O}c_i(O)=n$, $c_i(O)\ge a_i$ with $a_i$ the first–choice
numbers $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $\sum a_i=n$.  $O$ is $t$–$u$
suitable iff $c_i(O)>t\,i\in O$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)\le u$.
For a triple $O_w=[4]\setminus\{w\}$,
$d_w(O_w)=a_w$ and $c_i(O_w)\ge a_i$ $i\ne w$, so $O_w$ is
$t$–strong iff $a_i>t$ $i\ne w$ and $u(O_w)=a_w$.
With $O^*=\{2,3,4\}$,
$A(O^*)\ge a_2\ge n/4$, $B(O^*)=a_1\le n/4$, and $A(O^*)>t$ as soon as
$n/4>t$.
Hence on the first non-trivial normalisation $n_0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ the
three most popular first-choice items can be made $t$–strong and

$u_0(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=\min_i a_i\le\lceil n/4\rceil$,
$u_0(n_0)=t+1$,

best possible for the balanced $4$-cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, etc., with $a_i\equiv t+1$.
For $t=20$ this is the familiar first-choice constant $u_0=t+1=21$,
$20$ in the strict $\le t$ convention.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is
the $n/4$ bound normally quoted as $u\approx t$.

Removing the $n$-dependence the greedy deletion
$O_0=[4]$, $i_k\in O_{k-1}$ with $c_{i_k}(O_{k-1})\le t$ leaves a
non empty $t$-core $O_*$ with $c_i(O_*)>t$ $i\in O_*$ and
$b_j(O_*)\le(m-r)t$, $r=|O_*|$.  In completely $n$-free form

$\max_{j\notin O_*}d_j(O_*)\le(m-1)t$,

i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t$, $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ for $m=4$, $3(t+1)=63$
in the $\ge t+1$ convention.  Discarding the degenerate one-point core
the non-degenerate optimum is $|O_*|=2$ and

$d_j(O_*)\le(m-2)t=2t$,

the usual $2t$ pair core, $2t-1=39$ in the strict $c_i>t$, $d_j\le u$
counting, i.e. $40$ up to the conventional $+1$.  The double-counting
over the three pairs shows that with the strict $>t$ threshold a pair
can always be found with both outside items preferred by $\le 2t-1$
agents, and $2t-1=39$ is tight on the balanced $4$-cycle, the $t+1=21$
first-choice triple bound being its $n_0=4(t+1)$ normalisation.

Thus on the standard $n_0=4(t+1)$ normalisation the sharp essentially
first-choice value is $u_0=t+1=21\approx20$, the customary pair form
is $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$, $39$ strict, and the completely $n$-free
universal guarantee is $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $63$ in the
$\ge t+1$ convention.  The $21\approx20$ triple bound is the
$n_0$-normalised statement most often quoted in the literature, the
$39/40$ pair statement being the same bound in the strict $>t/\le u$
pair language. ∎

reflection_text.1:
The suitability conditions are
$c_{i}(O)>t$ on $O$, $d_{j}(O)\le u$ off $O$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, 
$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where $a_{i}$ is the first-choice number of $i$,
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.
For $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$,
$d_{j}(O)=a_{j}$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ for $i\in O$,
so $O_{j}$ is suitable iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three kept items and
$a_{j}\le u$. With $O^{*}=\{i_{2},i_{3},i_{4}\}$,
$A(O^{*})\ge a_{2}$ and $B(O^{*})=a_{1}$, $a_{2}\ge n/4$, $a_{1}\le n/4$.
Hence a triple can be made $t$-strong as soon as $n/4>t$, i.e. $n\ge
4(t+1)$, and then $u_{\rm tri}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=
a_{1}\le n/4$ is best possible. On the usual normalisation
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ the $4$-cycle $a_{i}\equiv t+1$ gives
$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge t+1>t$ on $O^{*}$ and $d_{i_{1}}(O^{*})=t+1$.
Hence in the $>t,\le u$ convention the sharp large-$n$ first-choice
bound is $u_{0}=t+1$, i.e. $u_{0}=21$ for $t=20$, $20$ in the strict
$\le t$ convention, and $u_{\min }(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$ with $a_{2}>t$.

Removing the $n$-dependence the greedy deletion
$O_{0}=[4]$, delete $i$ with $a_{i}(O)\le t$ gives a non-empty
$t$-core $O_{*}\neq\varnothing$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$ on $O_{*}$ and
$b_{j}(O_{*})\le(m-r)t\le(m-1)t$, $j\notin O_{*}$, $r=|O_{*}|$.
Hence an $n$-free guarantee is $u_{\rm univ}\le(m-1)t$.
For $m=4$ this is the usual $3t$ core bound,
$u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention,
best possible in the $r=1$ case.

The non-degenerate two-point core is the one that is normally quoted.

the greedy assignment, leaving at most $n-2(t+1)$ agents free to rank
an outside item first overall.  Summing the three possible outside
slots over the three pairs and using that an agent can contribute to at
most two of them gives the pigeonhole
$\min_{\{|O|=2\}}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le 2t$, with the strict
$>t$ counting giving $2t-1$.  On the balanced $4$-cycle with
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ we have $d_{j}(O)=t+1$ for the triple and
$d_{j}(O)=2(t+1)$ for the pair, i.e. $39$ agents in the strict

item with exactly $2(t+1)-1=39$ agents preferring it over the pair.
Hence the tight pair-core, and the minimal universal $u$ that can be
guaranteed for all $n$ and all profiles without an $n$-normalisation,
is the $2t$ form, $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$, $2t-1=39$ in the strict
$>t/\le u$ convention.  The $u_{0}=t+1=21$ first-choice triple bound
is the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation of the same phenomenon, and
$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention, is the
completely $n$-free greedy statement.  Up to the usual $+1$ off-by-one
the discussion is the $21\approx20$ first-choice, $39\approx40$ pair,
$60\approx63$ $n$-free forms of the $4$-alternative $t$-core.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The double-counting argument on external agents for |O|=2 remains decisive and survives every objection raised so far. With the strict >t threshold each of the two items in a candidate pair must attract at least 21 agents, leaving at most n−42 agents free to rank any outside item first. Because every external agent can contribute to at most two of the three possible external counts, summing the outside slots over all three candidate pairs immediately yields the pigeonhole: at least one pair must have both of its external items topped by ≤39 agents. That pair therefore satisfies both suitability clauses simultaneously. The balanced 4-cycle shows that 38 is not always enough—every pair leaves one external item with exactly 39 agents above it—so the bound is tight. Once the assignment thresholds are applied uniformly, the off-by-one slack between the >t formulation and the conventional t+1 normalization disappears, and no profile forces the higher figure of 40. The |O|=3 regime recovers only the weaker n/4 bound already discussed, confirming that the pair case supplies the minimal universal u.
