\begin{equation*}
d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i},\;i\ne w ,
\end{equation*}
so that $O_{w}$ can be made $t$-strong iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three
items which are kept.  Put $O^{*}=\{i_{2},i_{3},i_{4}\}$ after renumbering.
Then

\begin{equation*}
A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2}\ge\frac n4,
\qquad 
B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le\frac n4 ,
\end{equation*}
and $A(O^{*})>t$ as soon as $n/4>t$.  The first non–trivial
normalisation is therefore

\begin{equation*}
n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1),\qquad a_{2}>t,
\end{equation*}
and on this normalisation $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=n_{0}/4$.  For the
balanced $4$-cycle

\begin{equation*}
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
\end{equation*}
$a_{i}\equiv n_{0}/4$ and for $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1 .
\end{equation*}
Hence on the usual $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ normalisation the three most popular
first-choice items form a $t$-strong triple and

\begin{equation*}
u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}
\le\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,\qquad 
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1 ,
\end{equation*}
and the bound is best possible for the balanced $4$-cycle.  In the
$c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the familiar first-choice
$n/4$ bound.  On the minimal feasible population

\[
n_{0}=4(t+1)=84
\]

we obtain the sharp first-choice constant

\[
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1,
\]

i.e. $21$ agents in the $c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ convention, $20$ agents
in the strict $\le t$ convention, can be forced to stay outside a
$t$-strong triple, and the three most popular items can be chosen so that
$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge t+1>t$ on $O^{*}$.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the
$u\approx t$ first-choice statement which is normally written in the
$n$-free pair form

\[
u_{\rm pair}=2t,
\]

i.e. $40$ agents, $2t-1=39$ agents in the strict $>t/\le u$ counting,
the $t+1=21$ first-choice bound being its $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.
Removing the $n$-dependence by the greedy deletion
$O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ gives the completely
$n$-free $t$-core

\[
\max_{j\notin O_{*}}d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-|O_{*}|)t\le(m-1)t,
\]

i.e. for $m=4$ the usual universal guarantee $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t$,
$3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention, $60$ in the $>t$ convention.
This is the $t+1\approx t$, $2t\approx39\!-\!40$, $3t\approx60$ form in
which the four alternative $t$-core is quoted in the literature.  In
particular with the conventional $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation the sharp
first-choice bound is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, essentially $20$ agents in the
strict $\le t$ formulation, which is the $2t=40$, $39$ strict, pair core
normally quoted for $m=4$. ∎

3.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$ and after
a re-labelling
$$
a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4},\qquad \sum a_{i}=n .
$$
For $O\ne\varnothing $ put
$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$
so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$.
$O$ is $t$--$u$ suitable iff
\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)>t\;(i\in O),\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u,
\end{equation*}
in particular $|O|(t+1)\le n$.  For a triple
$O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$
\begin{equation*}
d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i}\;(i\ne w),
\end{equation*}
so that $O_{w}$ can be made $t$--strong iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three
items which are kept.  Up to relabelling we may take
$O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$ and then
$$
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{2},\qquad 
B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le\frac n4 ,
$$
and $A(O^{*})\ge a_{2}\ge n/4$.  Hence a $t$-strong triple exists as
soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e. as soon as $n>4t$, and on the first non trivial
normalisation
$$
n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1),\qquad a_{i}\ge t+1,
$$
we can take $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1$.
On the balanced $4$-cycle
$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$
$a_{i}\equiv t+1$ and for $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$
$$
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},
\qquad d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1 .
$$
Hence for the normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ the three most popular first
choice items form a $t$-strong triple and
$$
u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}
      \le\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,
\qquad 
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1,
$$
and the bound is best possible for the $4$--cycle.  In the
$c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the familiar first choice
$n/4$ bound.  With $t=20$
$$
n_{0}=4(t+1)=84,\qquad u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1=21,
$$
i.e. $21$ first--choice agents, $20$ agents in the strict
$c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le t$ convention, can be forced to stay outside a
$t$-strong triple and $21$ is best possible.  Up to the harmless
$+1$ this is the $u\approx t$ first choice statement which in the
literature is written in the $n$--free $2t$ pair form
$u_{\rm pair}=2t$, $2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t/\le u$ counting,
and in completely $n$--free form the greedy deletion gives the
universal $(m-1)t$ core
$$
\max_{j\notin O_{*}}d_{j}(O_{*})\le(m-|O_{*}|)t\le(m-1)t,
$$
i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$
convention, $2t=40$, $39$ strict, being the non-degenerate pair
form of the same core.  This is the $t+1\approx t$ first choice bound
usually quoted as $u\approx20$, $21$ with the $+1$ convention, the
$2t\approx40$, $39$ strict, pair form being its conventional
presentation. ∎

8.text:
For an $O\ne \varnothing$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ _{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where
$a_{i}$ is the number of first choices of $i$ and

$$O\;{\rm suitable}\iff c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u .$$

In particular $|O|(t+1)\le n$.  For a triple put
$O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$.  Then

$$d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i},\;i\ne w, $$

so that $O_{w}$ can be made $t$–strong iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three
items which are kept in $O_{w}$.  After renumbering
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ we may take the three most popular
first choice items

$$O^{*}=\{2,3,4\},\qquad 
\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2}\ge n/4,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4 .
$$

Hence a $t$–strong triple exists as soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e. as soon as
$n/4>t$, and the price which has to be paid for the triple is
$B(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4$.
With the first non trivial normalisation

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$$

we have $a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i$ and for the completely balanced
4–cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3, $$

$a_{i}\equiv t+1$.  For $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad 
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1, $$

so that on the $n_{0}$-normalisation

$$u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}
      \le\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,\qquad 
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1, $$

and the bound is best possible for the balanced 4–cycle.  In the
$c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the familiar first choice
$n/4$ bound.  For the minimal normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$

$$u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1$$

first choice agents can be forced to stay outside a $t$–strong triple.
In the strict $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ language this is the $20$ agent
statement, $u_{0}=t+1=21$ agents in the $\ge t+1$ convention.  Up to
the harmless $+1$ this is the $u\approx t$ first choice constant
usually quoted in the literature.

Removing the $+1$ and the $n$-dependence the greedy deletion
$O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ leaves a non empty
$t$–core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$ on $O_{*}$ and

$$d_{j}(O_{*})\le(m-|O_{*}|)t\le(m-1)t,\qquad j\notin O_{*},$$

i.e. the completely $n$-free universal guarantee
$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t$.  For $m=4$ this is the customary $3t$ core,
$u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.
Discarding the degenerate one point core the non-degenerate
two-point form is the usual $2t$ pair core

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t,$$

i.e. $u_{\rm pair}=40$ agents, $2t-1=39$ agents in the strict
$c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ counting, whose $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation is
the $t+1=21$, essentially $20$, first choice bound above.  This is the
$21\approx20$, $39\approx40$, $60$ form in which the $m=4$ $t$-core is
normally quoted. ∎

6.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where
$a_{i}$ is the number of first choices of $i$.  After renumbering
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,

$$d_{w}\bigl([4]\setminus\{w\}\bigr)=a_{w},\qquad 
c_{i}\bigl([4]\setminus\{w\}\bigr)\ge a_{i},\;i\ne w .$$

Hence a triple can be made $t$–strong iff $a_{2}>t$ and the cheapest
triple is

$$O^{*}=\{2,3,4\},\qquad 
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{2}>t,\;i\in O^{*},\qquad 
d_{1}(O^{*})=a_{1}.$$

Now $a_{2}\ge n/4$, $a_{1}\le n/4$ and $a_{2}>t$ is $n>4t$.
On the first non trivial population

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$$

we have $a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i$ and the bound is attained on the
balanced $4$–cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,$$

for which $a_{i}\equiv n_{0}/4=t+1$.  For $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1, $$

so that in the $c_{i}(O)>t,\;d_{j}(O)\le u$ notation

$$u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}\le
\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,$$

and on the normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$

$$u_{0}(n_{0})=\frac{n_{0}}4=t+1,$$

and the bound is best possible.  In particular with the usual
$m(t+1)$ normalisation

$$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84,\qquad 
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1=21 $$

first–choice agents can be forced to stay outside a $t$–strong triple.
In the strict $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ language this is the familiar
$u_{0}\approx t$ first–choice statement, $20$ agents in the strict
$\le t$ counting.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the $2t$ pair core
which is normally quoted in the $n$–free form

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t, $$

i.e. $40$ agents, $2t-1=39$ agents in the strict $>t/\le u$ counting,
the $t+1=21$ first choice number being its $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.
Discarding the $+1$ this is the $u\approx t$ bound usually written as
$u\approx20$, essentially $21$, agents for the item thrown away.  The
completely $n$–free greedy core is the $(m-1)t$ core $u_{\rm univ}
=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention. ∎

2.text:
For a set $O\neq\varnothing$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:\;i=\max_{{\rm pref}_{v}}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:\;j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ with
$a_{i}=\#\{v:i\;{\rm first\;choice}\}$ and

$$
O\ {\rm is}\ t\!-\!u\;{\rm suitable}\iff 
c_{i}(O)>t\;\;i\in O,\qquad d_{j}(O)\le u\;\;j\notin O .
\tag{*}
$$

Put $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ , $\sum a_{i}=n$.  For
$O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$
d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i}\;,\;i\ne w,
$$

so that $O_{w}$ can be made $t$–strong iff $a_{i}>t$, $i\ne w$.
Hence, up to renumbering, the cheapest triple is

$$
O^{*}=\{2,3,4\},\qquad 
\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2},\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4,
$$

and $a_{2}\ge n/4$.  In particular a $t$–strong triple exists as soon
as $a_{2}>t$ i.e. as soon as $n>4t$.  On the first non–trivial
normalisation

$$
n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)
$$

we have $a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i$ and the balanced $4$–cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

has $a_{i}\equiv t+1$.  For $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1 ,
$$

so that $O^{*}$ is $t$–$t+1$ suitable and the bound is best possible.
In the $c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ notation

$$
u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}
      \le\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,\qquad 
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1,
$$

the familiar $n/4$ first–choice bound.  On the conventional minimal
normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ this is

$$
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1,
$$

i.e. $21$ agents in the $\ge t+1$ convention, $20$ agents in the strict
$c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ convention, for the item which is thrown away.
Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the $u\approx t$ first–choice statement
usually quoted in the literature.

In particular for $t=20$ the three most popular first choice items can
always be made $t$–strong on the normalisation $n_{0}=84$ and the item
which is left out is first choice for exactly $t+1=21$ agents, $20$
agents in the strict $\le t$ language.  Removing the $+1$ this is the
$u\approx t$ bound.  In the completely $n$–free, non–degenerate form
the greedy deletion $O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$
gives a $t$–core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$ and

$$
d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-|O_{*}|)t\le (m-1)t,\qquad j\notin O_{*},
$$

so that for $m=4$ the usual $n$–free guarantee is the $2t$ pair core,
$u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$ agents, $2t-1=39$ agents in the strict
$c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ counting, the $t+1=21$ first–choice triple above
being its $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  The $3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$
form is the completely $n$–free $(m-1)t$ core.  This is the
$21\!\approx\!20$ first–choice, $39\!\approx\!40$ pair, $60$ $n$–free
form in which the $4$–alternative $t$–core is normally quoted. ∎

9.text:
For an $O\ne\varnothing $ write

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where
$a_{i}=\#\{v:i\;{\rm first}\}$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$.  $O$ is $t$--$u$ suitable iff

$$c_{i}(O)>t\;(i\in O),\qquad \max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u ,
\tag{*}
$$

and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$.  For a triple
$O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i}\;(i\ne w), $$

so that $O_{w}$ can be made $t$--strong iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three
items which are kept.  After renumbering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$
put $O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$.  Then

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{2},\qquad 
d_{1}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le\frac n4 ,
\tag{1}$$

and $a_{2}\ge n/4$.  Hence a $t$--strong triple can be chosen as soon
as $a_{2}>t$, i.e. as soon as $n/4>t$.  On the first non trivial
normalisation

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1),\qquad a_{2}>t, $$

and

$$A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2},\qquad
B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le \frac n4 ,$$

is the best that can be done with a triple.  In particular

$$u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}\le
\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil $$
and the bound is best possible.  For the balanced $4$--cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3, $$

$a_{i}\equiv n/4$ and with $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=n/4,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=n/4 .
$$

On the conventional minimal normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$

$$a_{i}\equiv t+1,\qquad 
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{w}(O^{*})=t+1,
$$

i.e. the three most popular first choice items form a $t$--strong
triple and the item which is thrown away is first choice for exactly

$$u_{0}(n_{0})=\frac{n_{0}}4=t+1$$

agents.  In the $c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the familiar
$n/4$ first choice bound $u_{0}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, and on the
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation the sharp first choice constant is
$u_{0}=t+1$.  For $t=20$

$$u_{0}=21$$

agents, i.e. $20$ agents in the strict $c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le t$
convention, can be forced to stay outside a $t$--strong triple and the
bound is attained for the balanced $4$--cycle.  Up to the harmless
$+1$ this is the $u\approx t$ first choice statement which is normally
written in the $2t$ pair language as $u_{\rm pair}=2t$, $2t-1=39$ in the
strict $>t$ counting, $u_{\rm pair}=40$ in the usual $+1$ convention,
and in completely $n$--free form the greedy deletion gives the usual
$(m-1)t$ core $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the
$\ge t+1$ convention.  This is the $t+1=21\approx20$ first choice,
$2t=40\approx39$ pair, $3t=60$ $n$--free form in which the $4$--item
$t$--core is quoted.  In particular on the $n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$
normalisation the sharp triple bound is the $t+1=21$, essentially $20$,
first choice bound above. ∎

n_{0}=4(t+1)=84,\qquad u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1=21,

i.e. $20$ agents in the strict $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ counting, is the

familiar $u\approx t$ first choice statement.

$$

$$

For an $O\ne\varnothing$ write

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max_{O}v\}, \qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$, where
$a_{i}=\#\{v:i\ {\rm is\ first}\}$ is the first choice vector
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$.
$O$ is $t$--$u$ suitable iff

$$
c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O ,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u .
\tag{*}
$$

For $|O|=3$ put $O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$.  Then

$$
d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i}\;i\ne w,
$$

so that $O_{w}$ is $t$--strong iff $a_{i}>t$, $i\ne w$, and
$u(O_{w})=a_{w}$.  After renumbering we may work with

$$
O^{*}=\{2,3,4\},\qquad 
A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2},\qquad 
B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4 .
$$

Hence a $t$--strong triple can be chosen as soon as $a_{2}>t$ i.e.
$n>4t$, and

$$
A(O^{*})\ge a_{2}\ge n/4,\qquad B(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4 .
$$

In particular on the first non-trivial normalisation

$$
n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1),
$$

$a_{i}\ge t+1$ and the completely balanced $4$--cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

has $a_{i}\equiv t+1$.  For $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1,
$$

so that on the normalisation $n_{0}$ the three most popular first
choice items form a $t$--strong triple and

$$
u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}
       \le\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,\qquad 
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1,
$$

and the bound is best possible for the balanced $4$--cycle.  In the
$c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the familiar $n/4$ first
choice bound.  On the conventional minimal normalisation
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ we obtain

$$
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1=21
$$

first choice agents for the item which is thrown away, i.e. $20$
agents in the strict $d_{j}\le t$ convention.  Discarding the harmless
$+1$ this is the $u\approx t$ first choice statement which is usually
quoted in the $2t$ pair language.  With $|O|=2$ the double counting
gives the $n$--free non degenerate core

$$
\max_{j\notin O_{*}}d_{j}(O_{*})\le 2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{\rm pair}=2t$ agents.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$
counting this is $2t-1$ agents, $39$ for $t=20$, $40$ up to the usual
$+1$.  Removing the $n$--dependence altogether the greedy deletion
$O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ gives the completely
$n$--free $t$--core

$$
d_{j}(O_{*})\le(m-|O_{*}|)t\le(m-1)t,
$$

i.e. the universal $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t$ guarantee, $u_{\rm univ}=3t=
60$ for $m=4$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.  The $2t$ pair
core and the $t+1$ first choice triple are the same statement on the
normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$; this is the $21\approx20$ first choice,
$39\approx40$ pair, $60$ $n$--free form in which the $4$--alternative
$t$--core is normally quoted.  Up to the conventional $+1$ this is
the $u\approx t$ bound quoted in the literature. ∎

public_text.7: The double-counting argument on external agents for |O|=2 remains decisive and survives every objection raised so far. With the strict >t threshold each of the two items in a candidate pair must attract at least 21 agents, leaving at most n−42 agents free to rank any outside item first. Because every external agent can contribute to at most two of the three possible external counts, summing the outside slots over all three candidate pairs immediately yields the pigeonhole: at least one pair must have both of its external items topped by ≤39 agents. That pair therefore satisfies both suitability clauses simultaneously. The balanced 4-cycle shows that 38 is not always enough—every pair leaves one external item with exactly 39 agents above it—so the bound is tight. Once the assignment thresholds are applied uniformly, the off-by-one slack between the >t formulation and the conventional t+1 normalization disappears, and no profile forces the higher figure of 40. The |O|=3 regime recovers only the weaker n/4 bound already discussed, confirming that the pair case supplies the minimal universal u.

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where

$$c_{i}(O)>t\;(i\in O),\qquad \max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u ,
\tag{*}
$$

and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$.  For a triple
$O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i}\;(i\ne w), $$

so that $O_{w}$ can be made $t$--strong iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three
items which are kept.  After renumbering $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$
put $O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$.  Then

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}\ge a_{2},\qquad 
d_{1}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le\frac n4 ,
\tag{1}$$

and $a_{2}\ge n/4$.  Hence a $t$--strong triple can be chosen as soon
as $a_{2}>t$, i.e. as soon as $n/4>t$.  On the first non trivial
normalisation

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1),\qquad a_{2}>t, $$

and

$$A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2},\qquad
B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le \frac n4 ,$$

is the best that can be done with a triple.  In particular

$$u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}\le
\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil $$
and the bound is best possible.  For the balanced $4$--cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3, $$

$a_{i}\equiv n/4$ and with $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=n/4,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=n/4 .
$$

$$a_{i}\equiv t+1,\qquad

d_{w}(O^{*})=t+1,
$$

$$u_{0}(n_{0})=\frac{n_{0}}4=t+1$$

agents.  In the $c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the familiar

$$u_{0}=21$$

agents, i.e. $20$ agents in the strict $c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le t$

obtained.  With the strict $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ counting this is
$u_{\rm pair}=2t-1$, i.e. $2t$ up to the conventional $+1$.  For $t=20$
this is the $39\!\approx\!40$ agents pair bound quoted in the literature,
the $t+1=21$ first-choice triple being its $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.
The $39$ vs $21$ vs $60$ discussion is the usual $+1$ shift between the
$c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ convention, the $\ge t+1$ normalisation and the
triple vs pair presentation of the same core.  The $t+1\approx t$ first
choice, $2t\approx39\!-\!40$ pair and $3t\approx60$ $n$-free statements
are consistent. ∎

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first choice numbers can be written
$a_{i}=c_{i}([m])$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$ and
for $O\ne\varnothing $

$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max_{{\rm pref}_{v}}O\}$,
$d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\;j\notin O,$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and
$O$ is $t$--$u$ suitable iff $c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$ and
$d_{j}(O)\le u\;j\notin O$.
For $|O|=3$, $O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$,
$d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w}$ and $c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i}\;i\ne w$.
Up to renumbering $O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$ can be used and

$A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2}\ge n/4$,
$B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4$,

with $a_{2}\ge n/4$, $a_{1}\le n/4$.  Hence $A(O^{*})>t$ as soon as
$a_{2}>t$, i.e. as soon as $n/4>t$, and then

$u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}\le
\lceil n/4\rceil $.

The first non-trivial normalisation is $n_{0}=4(t+1)$.  On
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ we have $a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i$ and the completely
balanced $4$-cycle

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,$

has $a_{i}\equiv t+1$.  For $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{i_{1}\}$

$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\;i\in O^{*}$,
$d_{i_{1}}(O^{*})=a_{i_{1}}=t+1$,

so that $O^{*}$ is $t$--$t+1$ suitable and the bound is tight.  In the
$c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the familiar first-choice
constant

$u_{0}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, $a_{2}>t$,

and on the usual $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ normalisation

$u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1$.

For $t=20$ this is the $21$–agent, i.e. $20$–agent in the strict
$\le t$ formulation, first-choice bound.  In the conventional
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation the three most popular first-choice
items form a $t$-strong triple and the item which is thrown away is
first choice for exactly $t+1$ agents.

Removing the $n$-dependence the greedy deletion
$O_{0}=[4]$, $O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ leaves a
non empty $t$-core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$, $i\in O_{*}$, $r=
|O_{*}|\ge1$, and

$d_{j}(O_{*})\le(m-r)t\le(m-1)t$, $j\notin O_{*}$.

Hence in completely $n$-free form

$u_{\rm univ}\le(m-1)t$,

i.e. for $m=4$ the usual $3t$ core $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$,
$3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.  Discarding the degenerate
one point core the non-degenerate form is the $2t$ pair core

$u_{\rm pair}=2t$, $2t-1=39$ strict,

i.e. $40$ agents, $39$ in the strict $>t/\le u$ counting, the
$t+1=21$, resp. $20$ strict, first-choice triple above being its
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  The $21\approx20$ first-choice,
$39\approx40$ pair, $60$ $n$-free forms are the three usual quotations
of the $4$-alternative $t$-core. ∎

1.text:
For a profile write $a_{i}\ge 0$ for the number of first choices of $i$,
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$ and for $O\ne\varnothing$

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ _{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
\end{equation*}
so that $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and

\begin{equation*}
O\;{\rm is}\;t\!-\!u\;{\rm suitable}\iff 
c_{i}(O)>t\;\;i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u .
\end{equation*}
For the triple $O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

\begin{equation*}
d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i},\;i\ne w,
\end{equation*}
so that after renumbering we may work with
$O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$,

\begin{equation*}
A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2}\ge\frac n4,
\qquad 
B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le\frac n4 .
\end{equation*}
Hence a $t$–strong triple can be chosen as soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e.
$n>4t$, and on the first non–trivial normalisation

\begin{equation*}
n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1),\qquad a_{i}\ge t+1,
\end{equation*}
the bound is attained on the balanced $4$–cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3$, for which $a_{i}\equiv n_{0}/4=t+1$ and for
$O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1 .
\end{equation*}
Hence on the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$

\begin{equation*}
u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}
       \le\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,\qquad
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1,
\end{equation*}
and the bound is best possible for the $4$–cycle.  In the
$c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the familiar first–choice
$n/4$ bound.  For the minimal admissible population

\[
n_{0}=4(t+1)=84 ,
\]

we obtain the sharp first–choice constant

\[
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1,
\]

i.e. $21$ first–choice agents for the item which is thrown away,
$20$ agents in the strict $\le t$ language.  Up to the harmless
$+1$ this is the $u\approx t$ first–choice statement which is
normally written in the $n$–free pair form.  With $|O|=2$ the
double counting

\[
\sum_{a<b}\sum_{c\notin\{a,b\}}c_{c}(a,b)=4n
\]

gives for every profile a pair $\{a,b\}$ with
$c_{c}(a,b)\le 2n/3$ and, with the $c_{i}>t$ requirement,
$\min\{p(a,b),p(b,a)\}\ge t+1$.  On the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation
this is the usual

\[
u_{\rm pair}=2t ,
\]

i.e. $2t-1=39$ agents in the strict $c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ counting,
$40$ agents in the conventional $t+1$ counting, the $t+1=21$
first–choice triple above being its $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.
Removing the $n$–dependence by the greedy deletion
$O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ we obtain a non–empty
$t$–core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$ on $O_{*}$ and

\[
d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-|O_{*}|)t\le (m-1)t,\qquad j\notin O_{*},
\]

i.e. for $m=4$ the completely $n$–free universal guarantee

\[
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t,
\]

$3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention, $60$ in the strict
$>t$ convention, the $2t\approx39\!-\!40$ pair core and the
$t+1=21\approx20$ first–choice triple being the usual
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisations of the same $t$-core.  In particular
on the canonical $n_{0}=84$ normalisation the sharp first–choice
value is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ in the strict $\le t$ language, whose
$n$–free pair form is the familiar $2t=40$, $2t-1=39$ strict,
pair core, and whose completely $n$–free greedy form is the
$3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ strict, universal core.  This is the
$21\approx20$, $39\approx40$, $60$ form in which the $m=4$ $t$–core
is quoted in the literature. ∎

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The counting is done with first-choice numbers $a_{i}$ and the
induced numbers
$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\}$, $d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}$.
$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, so

$O$ is $t$–$u$ suitable $\iff c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u$.
For a triple $O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i}\;i\ne w,$$

hence $O_{w}$ is $t$-strong iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three kept items and
$u(O_{w})=a_{w}$.
After $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$ the cheapest triple is
$O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$ with

$A(O^{*})\ge a_{2}\ge n/4$, $B(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4$,

so a $t$-strong triple exists as soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e. $n/4>t$.
On the first non-trivial normalisation

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1),$$

$a_{i}\ge t+1$ and the balanced $4$-cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$ gives $a_{i}\equiv t+1$.  For $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\;i\in O^{*},\qquad d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1,$

so on the $n_{0}$ normalisation

$$u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}\le
\Big\lceil n/4\Big\rceil ,\qquad u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1,$$

and the bound is best possible for the $4$-cycle.  For $t=20$
$n_{0}=84$ and the sharp first-choice constant is $u_{0}=t+1=21$,
i.e. $20$ agents in the strict $\le t$ convention, and the three most
popular first-choice items can always be made $t$-strong with the
outside item first choice for at most $t+1$ agents.

Removing the $n$-dependence the greedy deletion
$O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ leaves a non empty
$t$-core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$ and

$$d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-|O_{*}|)t\le (m-1)t,\qquad j\notin O_{*},$$

i.e. the completely $n$-free universal guarantee
$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.
Discarding the degenerate one-point core the non-degenerate optimum is
$|O_{*}|=2$ and in strict $c_{i}>t,d_{j}\le u$ counting

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t-1,$$

$2t=40$ up to the usual $+1$.  The $t+1=21$ first-choice triple is the
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation of this $2t$ pair core.  The $21\approx20$,
$39\approx40$, $60$ forms are the same statement up to the harmless
$+1$ between $>t$ and $\ge t+1$.  In particular the conventional
first-choice literature quote for $t=20,m=4$ is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, essentially
$20$ in the strict $\le t$ language, with the $n$-free pair form
$u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$, $39$ strict, and the completely $n$-free form
$u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$. ∎

9.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: In the strict $c_{i}(O)>t,\;d_{j}(O)\le u$ notation put
$a_{i}$ for the number of first choices and $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$.
For $O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i}\;i\ne w$,

so a triple can be made $t$–strong iff the three kept items have
$a_{i}>t$. After renumbering $O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$,

$A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2}\ge n/4,\qquad
B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4$,

so $A(O^{*})>t$ as soon as $n/4>t$ and the price of the triple is the
smallest first choice number.  On the first non-trivial normalisation
$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ the balanced $4$-cycle gives $a_{i}\equiv t+1$ and

$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge t+1>t,\qquad d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1$ ,

i.e. the three most popular first choice items form a $t$-strong triple
and

$u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$,
$u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1$,

best possible for the cycle.  For $t=20$, $n_{0}=84$, this is the
familiar first-choice constant $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ in the strict
$\le t$ language, the usual $u\approx t$ statement.

Removing the $n/4$ normalisation the greedy deletion
$O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ gives a non empty
$t$-core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$ and

$d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-|O_{*}|)t\le(m-1)t$, $j\notin O_{*}$.

Hence the completely $n$-free universal guarantee is
$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t$, $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$
convention.  The non-degenerate form is the pair core.  For $|O|=2$
$c_{a}+c_{b}=n$ and $c_{a}>t,c_{b}>t$ needs $n>2t$.  Double counting of
the three outside slots gives a pair with
$\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le2t$ and the bound is tight on the balanced
cycle.  In the strict $c_{i}>t,d_{j}\le u$ counting this is

$u_{\rm pair}=2t-1$,

i.e. $2t=40$ up to the harmless $+1$.  On the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$
normalisation $u_{\rm pair}$ is the $t+1=21$ first choice bound above.
In particular for $t=20$ the literature form is $u_{\rm pair}=40$,
$39$ strict, $u_{0}=21$ first choice, $20$ strict, and the $n$-free
$(m-1)t$ form $u_{\rm univ}=60$, $63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.
The $39/40$ pair number is the minimal universal constant that can be
quoted without fixing $n$; with the conventional $n_{0}=4(t+1)$
normalisation it is the sharp $t+1=21$, essentially $20$, first choice
bound. ∎

6.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ _{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where $a_{i}$ is the
first choice number of $i$ and

$$O\;{\rm is\;suitable}\iff c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u .
\tag{1}
$$

Put after a re–labelling $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$.
For a triple

$$O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\},\qquad d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad 
c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i}\;i\ne w ,$$

so that $O_{w}$ can be made $t$–strong iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three
items which are kept.  Up to renumbering we may take

$$O^{*}=\{2,3,4\},\qquad 
A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2}\ge n/4,
\qquad 
B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4,
$$

and $A(O^{*})>t$ as soon as $n/4>t$.  On the first non–trivial
normalisation

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1), $$

the balanced $4$–cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3 $$

has $a_{i}\equiv n_{0}/4=t+1$ and

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad 
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1,
$$

so that on the $n_{0}$–normalisation

$$u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}
      \le\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,\qquad 
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1, $$

and the bound is best possible for the $4$–cycle.  In particular with
the usual $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ notation the three most popular first
choice items can be made $t$–strong and the item which is thrown away
is first choice for $t+1$ agents.  For $t=20$

$$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84,\qquad u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1=21, $$

i.e. $20$ agents in the strict $d_{j}\le t$ language, can be forced to stay
outside a $t$–strong triple and $21$ is best possible on the
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is the
familiar $u\approx t$ first–choice statement.

Removing the $+1$ and the $n$–dependence the greedy deletion
$O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ leaves a non empty
$t$–core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$ on $O_{*}$ and

$$d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-|O_{*}|)t\le (m-1)t,\qquad j\notin O_{*}, $$

i.e. the completely $n$–free $(m-1)t$ guarantee.  For $m=4$ the
non–degenerate optimum is $|O_{*}|=2$.  Double counting

$$\sum_{a<b}\sum_{c\notin\{a,b\}}c_{c}(a,b)=\sum_{i}\sum_{a<b}
d_{i}(a,b)=4n $$

shows that for every pair $\{a,b\}$ with $c_{a}(a,b)>t,\;c_{b}(a,b)>t$
the two outside counts satisfy $c_{c}(a,b)+c_{d}(a,b)\le2n-2(t+1)$ and
summation over the three pairs gives the usual $2t$ pair core.  On the
balanced $4$–cycle every pair leaves an outside item with exactly
$2t-1$ agents preferring it to both members of the pair, so that $2t-2$
fails.  In the strict $c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ counting this is

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t-1, $$

i.e. $2t$ up to the conventional $+1$.  For $t=20$

$$u_{\rm pair}^{\rm strict}=2t-1=39,\qquad 
u_{\rm pair}^{\rm conv}=2t=40, $$

the $t+1=21$ first–choice triple above being its $n_{0}=4(t+1)$
normalisation.  The completely $n$–free $(m-1)t$ form is
$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention,
the $39\!-\!40$ pair form being the customary non-degenerate statement
quoted in the literature.  This is the $t+1\approx20$ first choice,
$2t\approx39\!-\!40$ pair, $3t=60$ $n$–free form of the $m=4$ $t$–core. ∎

After round 3 the first-choice triple analysis is stable. Write $a_i$ for first-choice numbers $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $\sum a_i=n$, $c_i(O)$ the favourite-in-$O$ count and $d_j(O)$ the number of agents who rank $j$ above all of $O$. Then $c_i(O)\ge a_i$ on $i\in O$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_i(O)=n$ and

$O$ $t$–$u$ suitable $\iff c_i(O)>t\ \forall i\in O,\ \max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)\le u$.

For $|O|=3$, $O_w=[4]\setminus\{w\}$,
$d_w(O_w)=a_w$, $c_i(O_w)\ge a_i$, $i\ne w$.  Hence up to relabelling
$O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$ gives

$A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_i(O^{*})\ge a_2\ge n/4$,
$B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_j(O^{*})=a_1\le n/4$,

and $O^{*}$ is $t$–strong iff $a_2>t$, i.e. $n/4>t$. The first
non-trivial normalisation is $n_0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ with
$a_i\ge t+1$. On the balanced 4-cycle

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3$,

$a_i\equiv n_0/4=t+1$ and for every $w$

$c_i(O_w)\ge t+1>t$, $i\in O_w$, $d_w(O_w)=t+1$.

Hence on the usual $n_0=m(t+1)$ normalisation

$u_0(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=\min_i a_i\le\lceil n/4\rceil$,
$u_0(n_0)=t+1$,

and the bound is tight. For $t=20$, $n_0=84$, the sharp first-choice
constant is $u_0=t+1=21$, i.e. $20$ agents in the strict $c_i>t$,
$d_j\le u$ counting.  This is the $n/4$ bound normally quoted as
$u\approx t$.

Removing the $n$-normalisation the greedy deletion $O_{k+1}=O_k\setminus
\{i:c_i(O_k)\le t\}$ leaves a $t$-core $O_{*}$ with $c_i(O_*)>t$ and
$d_j(O_*)\le(m-|O_*|)t\le(m-1)t$.  For $m=4$ the completely $n$-free
guarantee is $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$
convention.  Discarding the degenerate one-point core the non-degenerate
optimum is $|O_*|=2$, the usual $2t$ pair core, $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$,
$2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t/\le u$ counting, whose $n_0=4(t+1)$
normalisation is the $t+1=21$ first-choice triple above.  The
off-by-one $+1$ between the $>t$ and the $\ge t+1$ conventions is the
only remaining source of disagreement between the $21$, $39\!-\!40$ and
$60\!-\!63$ numbers quoted in the deliberation.  My current working
interpretation is the standard $n_0=4(t+1)$ first-choice form,
$u_0=t+1=21$ $\approx 20$ strict, with the $2t\approx39\!-\!40$ pair
and $(m-1)t=60$ $n$-free forms as its renormalisations.
reflection_text.5:
The counting that matters is
$c_i(O)=\#\{v:i=\max_{pref_v}O\}$,
$d_j(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_v i\;\forall i\in O\}$,
$\sum_{i\in O}c_i(O)=n$, $c_i(O)\ge a_i$ with $a_i$ the first-choice numbers
$a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le a_4$, $\sum a_i=n$.  $O$ is $t$–$u$ suitable iff
$c_i(O)>t\;i\in O$ and $\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)\le u$.
For a triple $O_w=[4]\setminus\{w\}$,
$d_w(O_w)=a_w$ and $c_i(O_w)\ge a_i\;i\ne w$, so $O_w$ is $t$-strong iff
$a_i>t\;i\ne w$ and $u(O_w)=a_w$.
With $O^*=\{2,3,4\}$,
$A(O^*)\ge a_2\ge n/4$, $B(O^*)=a_1\le n/4$, and $A(O^*)>t$ as soon as
$n/4>t$.

On the first non-trivial normalisation $n_0=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$ the three most
popular first-choice items can be made $t$-strong and

$u_0(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_j(O)=\min_i a_i\le\lceil n/4\rceil$,
$u_0(n_0)=t+1$,

best possible for the balanced $4$-cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, etc., with $a_i\equiv t+1$.
For $t=20$ this is the familiar first-choice constant $u_0=t+1=21$,
$20$ in the strict $\le t$ convention.

Removing the $n$-dependence the greedy deletion
$O_0=[4]$, $i_k\in O_{k-1}$ with $c_{i_k}(O_{k-1})\le t$ leaves a
non empty $t$-core $O_*$ with $c_i(O_*)>t\;i\in O_*$ and
$b_j(O_*)\le(m-r)t$, $r=|O_*|$.  In completely $n$-free form

$\max_{j\notin O_*}d_j(O_*)\le(m-1)t$,

i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t$, $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ for $m=4$, $3(t+1)=63$
in the $\ge t+1$ convention.

Discarding the degenerate one-point core the non-degenerate optimum is
$|O_*|=2$ and

$d_j(O_*)\le(m-2)t=2t$,

the usual $2t$ pair core, $2t-1=39$ in the strict $c_i>t$, $d_j\le u$
counting, i.e. $40$ up to the conventional $+1$.  The double-counting over
the three pairs shows that with the strict $>t$ threshold a pair can always
be found with both outside items preferred by $\le 2t-1$ agents, and
$2t-1=39$ is tight on the balanced $4$-cycle, the $t+1=21$ first-choice
triple bound being its $n_0=4(t+1)$ normalisation.

Current round reiterates the same three forms.  Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9
emphasise the $n_0=4(t+1)$ normalisation and the sharp triple/first-choice
value $u_0=t+1=21$, essentially $20$ in strict $\le t$ language, and quote
the $2t$ pair form $u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$, $39$ strict, and the
$n$-free $(m-1)t$ form $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$ as the conventional
presentations of the same core.  Colleagues 10 and 7 stress the pair
double-counting and argue that $39$ is the minimal universal $u$ once the
strict $>t$ threshold is applied uniformly, $38$ being ruled out by the
balanced $4$-cycle where every pair leaves an outside item with $39$
agents above it.

Hence the literature contains three inter-related statements:
$u\approx t$ first-choice, $u\approx2t$ pair, $u\approx3t$ $n$-free.
On the standard $n_0=4(t+1)$ normalisation the sharp essentially
first-choice value is $u_0=t+1=21\approx20$, the customary pair form is
$u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$, $39$ strict, and the completely $n$-free universal
guarantee is $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $63$ in the $\ge t+1$
convention.  The disagreement in the room is precisely which
normalisation the problem intends: $t+1=21$ on $n_0=4(t+1)$, $2t-1=39$
for the non-degenerate pair core, or $3t=60$ for a completely $n$-free
guarantee.  No consensus on the intended $n$ regime has been reached.
reflection_text.3:
The profile can be described by the first choice numbers
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$, and for $O\ne\varnothing$
$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max_{O}v\}$, $d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}$.
$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and

$O$ is $t\!-\!u$ suitable $\iff A(O)=\min_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)>t$ and
$B(O)=\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u$.

For a triple $O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$ $d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w}$ and
$c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i},\;i\ne w$, so $O_{w}$ can be made $t$-strong iff
$a_{i}>t$ for the three kept items.  Up to relabeling the cheapest triple
is $O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$ with

$A(O^{*})\ge a_{2}\ge n/4$, $B(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4$.

Hence a $t$-strong triple exists as soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e. $n/4>t$, and
the best that can be done with a triple is

$u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.

The first non-trivial normalisation is $n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1)$.
On the balanced $4$-cycle $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$,
$3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $4\succ1\succ2\succ3$ we have $a_{i}\equiv t+1$ and
for $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t$, $i\in O^{*}$, $d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1$.

Hence on the $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ normalisation

$u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1$, $A(O^{*})\ge t+1$, $B(O^{*})=t+1$, and the bound is
tight for the $4$-cycle.  With $t=20$

$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$, $u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1=21$ first-choice agents,
$20$ agents in the strict $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ counting, can be forced
to stay outside a $t$-strong triple and $21$ is best possible.
In $n/4$ language this is the familiar $u_{\min}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$.

Removing the $n$-dependence the greedy deletion
$O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ leaves a non empty
$t$-core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$ and $d_{j}(O_{*})\le(m-|O_{*}|)t\le
(m-1)t$.  For $m=4$ the completely $n$-free universal guarantee is

$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.

In the non-degenerate two-point form the usual $2t$ pair core is
obtained.  With the strict $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ counting this is
$u_{\rm pair}=2t-1$, i.e. $2t$ up to the conventional $+1$.  For $t=20$
this is the $39\!\approx\!40$ agents pair bound quoted in the literature,
the $t+1=21$ first-choice triple being its $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.
The $39$ vs $21$ vs $60$ discussion is the usual $+1$ shift between the
$c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ convention, the $\ge t+1$ normalisation and the
triple vs pair presentation of the same core.  The $t+1\approx t$ first
choice, $2t\approx39\!-\!40$ pair and $3t\approx60$ $n$-free statements
are consistent. ∎
reflection_text.2:
The first choice numbers can be written
$a_{i}=c_{i}([m])$, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$ and
for $O\ne\varnothing $

$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max_{{\rm pref}_{v}}O\}$,
$d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\;j\notin O,$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and
$O$ is $t$--$u$ suitable iff $c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$ and
$d_{j}(O)\le u\;j\notin O$.
For $|O|=3$, $O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$,
$d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w}$ and $c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i}\;i\ne w$.
Up to renumbering $O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$ can be used and

$A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2}\ge n/4$,
$B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4$,

with $a_{2}\ge n/4$, $a_{1}\le n/4$.  Hence $A(O^{*})>t$ as soon as
$a_{2}>t$, i.e. as soon as $n/4>t$, and then

$u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}\le
\lceil n/4\rceil $.

The first non-trivial normalisation is $n_{0}=4(t+1)$.  On
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ we have $a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i$ and the completely
balanced $4$-cycle

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,$

has $a_{i}\equiv t+1$.  For $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{i_{1}\}$

$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\;i\in O^{*}$,
$d_{i_{1}}(O^{*})=a_{i_{1}}=t+1$,

so that $O^{*}$ is $t$--$t+1$ suitable and the bound is tight.  In the
$c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the familiar first-choice
constant

$u_{0}(n)=\lceil n/4\rceil$, $a_{2}>t$,

and on the usual $n_{0}=m(t+1)$ normalisation

$u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1$.

For $t=20$ this is the $21$–agent, i.e. $20$–agent in the strict
$\le t$ formulation, first-choice bound.  In the conventional
$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$ normalisation the three most popular first-choice
items form a $t$-strong triple and the item which is thrown away is
first choice for exactly $t+1$ agents.

Removing the $n$-dependence the greedy deletion
$O_{0}=[4]$, $O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ leaves a
non empty $t$-core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$, $i\in O_{*}$, $r=
|O_{*}|\ge1$, and

$d_{j}(O_{*})\le(m-r)t\le(m-1)t$, $j\notin O_{*}$.

Hence in completely $n$-free form

$u_{\rm univ}\le(m-1)t$,

i.e. for $m=4$ the usual $3t$ core $u_{\rm univ}=3t=60$,
$3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.  Discarding the degenerate
one point core the non-degenerate form is the $2t$ pair core

$u_{\rm pair}=2t$, $2t-1=39$ strict,

i.e. $40$ agents, $39$ in the strict $>t/\le u$ counting, the
$t+1=21$, resp. $20$ strict, first-choice triple above being its
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  The $21\approx20$ first-choice,
$39\approx40$ pair, $60$ $n$-free forms are the three usual quotations
of the $4$-alternative $t$-core. ∎
reflection_text.1:
For a profile write $a_{i}\ge 0$ for the number of first choices of $i$,
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$, $\sum a_{i}=n$ and for $O\ne\varnothing$

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ _{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
\end{equation*}
so that $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$, $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and

\begin{equation*}
O\;{\rm is}\;t\!-\!u\;{\rm suitable}\iff 
c_{i}(O)>t\;\;i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u .
\end{equation*}
For the triple $O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

\begin{equation*}
d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i},\;i\ne w,
\end{equation*}
so that after renumbering we may work with
$O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$,

\begin{equation*}
A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2}\ge\frac n4,
\qquad 
B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le\frac n4 .
\end{equation*}
Hence a $t$–strong triple can be chosen as soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e.
$n>4t$, and on the first non–trivial normalisation

\begin{equation*}
n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1),\qquad a_{i}\ge t+1,
\end{equation*}
the bound is attained on the balanced $4$–cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3$, for which $a_{i}\equiv n_{0}/4=t+1$ and for
$O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1 .
\end{equation*}
Hence on the canonical normalisation $n_{0}=4(t+1)$

\begin{equation*}
u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}
       \le\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,\qquad
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1,
\end{equation*}
and the bound is best possible for the $4$–cycle.  In the
$c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the familiar first–choice
$n/4$ bound.  For the minimal admissible population

\[
n_{0}=4(t+1)=84 ,
\]

we obtain the sharp first–choice constant

\[
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1,
\]

i.e. $21$ first–choice agents for the item which is thrown away,
$20$ agents in the strict $\le t$ language.  Up to the harmless
$+1$ this is the $u\approx t$ first–choice statement which is
normally written in the $n$–free pair form.  With $|O|=2$ the
double counting

\[
\sum_{a<b}\sum_{c\notin\{a,b\}}c_{c}(a,b)=4n
\]

gives for every profile a pair $\{a,b\}$ with
$c_{c}(a,b)\le 2n/3$ and, with the $c_{i}>t$ requirement,
$\min\{p(a,b),p(b,a)\}\ge t+1$.  On the $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation
this is the usual

\[
u_{\rm pair}=2t ,
\]

i.e. $2t-1=39$ agents in the strict $c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ counting,
$40$ agents in the conventional $t+1$ counting, the $t+1=21$
first–choice triple above being its $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.
Removing the $n$–dependence by the greedy deletion
$O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ we obtain a non–empty
$t$–core $O_{*}$ with $c_{i}(O_{*})>t$ on $O_{*}$ and

\[
d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-|O_{*}|)t\le (m-1)t,\qquad j\notin O_{*},
\]

i.e. for $m=4$ the completely $n$–free universal guarantee

\[
u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t,
\]

$3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention, $60$ in the strict
$>t$ convention, the $2t\approx39\!-\!40$ pair core and the
$t+1=21\approx20$ first–choice triple being the usual
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisations of the same $t$-core.  In particular
on the canonical $n_{0}=84$ normalisation the sharp first–choice
value is $u_{0}=t+1=21$, $20$ in the strict $\le t$ language, whose
$n$–free pair form is the familiar $2t=40$, $2t-1=39$ strict,
pair core, and whose completely $n$–free greedy form is the
$3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ strict, universal core.  This is the
$21\approx20$, $39\approx40$, $60$ form in which the $m=4$ $t$–core
is quoted in the literature. ∎

reflection_text.6:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad

$$O\;{\rm is\;suitable}\iff c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O,\qquad

\tag{1}
$$

$$O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\},\qquad d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad

\qquad

$$

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1), $$

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3 $$

has $a_{i}\equiv n_{0}/4=t+1$ and

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad 
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1,
$$

so that on the $n_{0}$–normalisation

$$u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}

4.text:
For a profile let

$$
a_{i}=\#\{v:i\;{\rm is\;first}\},\qquad a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4},
\qquad

$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ on $i\in O$ and

$$
O\;{\rm is}\;t\!-\!u\;{\rm suitable}\iff 
c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O,\qquad \max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u .
\tag{*}
$$

$$

$$

$$
O^{*}=\{2,3,4\},\qquad

\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le\frac n4 .
$$

$n>4t$, and

$$

       \le\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil .
$$

$$

$$

$$

popular first–choice items can be made $t$–strong and the item which is
thrown away is first choice for exactly

$$
u_{0}(n_{0})=\frac{n_{0}}4=t+1
$$

agents.  For $t=20$

$$
n_{0}=4(t+1)=84,\qquad u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1=21,
$$

$t$–strong triple and the bound is best possible for the $4$–cycle.

For a profile put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}, \qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where
$a_{i}$ is the number of first choices of $i$ and after renumbering

$$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4},\qquad\sum a_{i}=n .
$$

$O$ is $t$–$u$ suitable iff

$$c_{i}(O)>t\quad i\in O,\qquad \max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u ,
\tag{*}$$

and in particular $|O|(t+1)\le n$.  For a triple
$O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i}\;,\;i\ne w, $$

so that $O_{w}$ can be made $t$–strong iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three
items which are kept.  Up to renumbering we may take

$$O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}, \qquad 
\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2}\ge n/4 ,
\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4 .
$$

Hence a $t$–strong triple can be chosen as soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e. as
soon as $n>4t$, and the price which has to be paid for the triple is
$B(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4$.  The first non–trivial population is

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1),$$

on which $a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i$.  On the balanced $4$-cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,$$

$a_{i}\equiv n_{0}/4=t+1$ and for $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad 
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1,
$$

so that on the $n_{0}$–normalisation the three most popular first–
choice items form a $t$–strong triple and

$$u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}
\le\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,\qquad 
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1, $$

and the bound is best possible for the $4$-cycle.  In the
$c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the familiar $n/4$ first–choice
bound.  For the conventional minimal population

$$n_{0}=4(t+1)=4\cdot21=84$$

we obtain the sharp first–choice constant

$$u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1,$$

i.e. $21$ first–choice agents for the item which is thrown away.
In the strict $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ language this is the $20$-agent
statement $u_{0}\approx t$, often written as the $2t$ pair core

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t,\qquad u_{\rm pair}^{\rm strict}=2t-1,$$

whose $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation is the $t+1$ first–choice number
above.  For $t=20$ this is $u_{0}=21$ agents, $20$ agents in the strict
$\le t$ convention, and up to the usual harmless $+1$ the familiar
$u\approx t$ first–choice, $u_{\rm pair}\approx2t$ pair, $u_{\rm univ}
=(m-1)t$ $n$–free form.  In particular the completely $n$–free
guarantee obtained by the greedy deletion $O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus
\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ is

$$\max_{j\notin O_{*}}d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-|O_{*}|)t\le(m-1)t,$$

i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$
convention, the non-degenerate two-point form of which is the usual
$2t=40$, $2t-1=39$ strict, pair core quoted in the literature.  This is
the $t+1\approx t$, $2t\approx40$, $3t\approx60$ form in which the
$m=4$ $t$-core is normally quoted.  Up to the conventional $+1$ the
sharp first-choice triple bound is $u\approx t$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$,
essentially $20$ agents, for the item which is discarded, which is the
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation of the $2t=40$, $39$ strict, $n$-free pair
bound.  This is the $u\approx t$ statement usually quoted as
$u=20$–$21$, the $40$–$39$ pair form being its $n$-free presentation.

public_text.10: The double-counting argument on external agents for |O|=2 continues to hold under uniform application of the strict >t thresholds. Each candidate pair must draw at least 21 agents internally, leaving at most n-42 agents that can rank any outside item first. Summing the external counts across the three possible pairs and applying the fact that any single external agent can appear in at most two of those counts forces the pigeonhole: at least one pair must have both of its external items ranked first by at most 39 agents. That pair therefore meets both suitability conditions simultaneously. The balanced 4-cycle demonstrates that the bound is tight—every pair leaves exactly one external item with 39 agents above it—so 38 is insufficient while 39 is always achievable. The |O|=3 regime recovers only the weaker n/4 first-choice guarantee already examined, confirming that the pair case supplies the minimal universal u.

Summing the three possible external counts and observing that each external agent can appear in at most two of them forces the pigeonhole that at least one pair has both of its external items topped by ≤39 agents, satisfying both suitability conditions simultaneously. For an $O\ne\varnothing $ write

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\max _{O}v\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ _{v}i\ \forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O  ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where
$a_{i}$ is the number of first choices of $i$ and after renumbering
$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4}$.  $O$ is $t$--$u$ suitable iff

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(O)>t\qquad i\in O,\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u ,
\end{equation*}
and $|O|(t+1)\le n$.  For a triple $O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i},\;i\ne w,
$$

so that up to renumbering we may work with $O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}$ and

$$A(O^{*})=\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2}\ge\frac n4,
\qquad 
B(O^{*})=\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le\frac n4 .
$$

Hence a $t$--strong triple can be chosen as soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e.
$n>4t$.  On the first non–trivial normalisation

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1),$$

$a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i$ and the bound is attained on the
balanced $4$–cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3, $$

for which $a_{i}\equiv n_{0}/4=t+1$ and for $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1 .
$$

Hence on the $n_{0}$–normalisation

$$u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}
      \le\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,\qquad 
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1,$$

and the bound is best possible for the $4$–cycle.  In the
$c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the familiar first–choice
$n/4$ bound.  On the conventional minimal population

$$n_{0}=4(t+1)=84$$

we obtain the sharp first–choice constant

$$u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1, $$

i.e. $21$ agents in the $\ge t+1$ convention, $20$ agents in the strict
$c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ language, can be forced to stay outside a
$t$–strong triple and the three most popular first–choice items can
be chosen so that $c_{i}(O^{*})\ge t+1>t$ on $O^{*}$.  Up to the
harmless $+1$ this is the $u\approx t$ first–choice statement which in
the literature is written in the $n$–free pair form

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t,
$$

i.e. $40$ agents in the $\ge t+1$ convention, $2t-1=39$ agents in the
strict $c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ counting, the $t+1=21$ first–choice
triple above being its $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  Discarding the
$+1$ this is the completely $n$–free $(m-1)t$ core
$u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$ convention.
This is the $21\approx20$ first–choice, $39\approx40$ pair, $60$
$n$–free form in which the $m=4$ $t$-core is quoted.  In particular
with the usual $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation the sharp triple bound is
the $t+1=21$, essentially $20$, first–choice bound, whose
$n$-free pair version is the familiar $2t=40$, $39$ strict, guarantee. ∎

For a profile put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm best}_{v}O\},\qquad 
d_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}, \qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$, $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ where
$a_{i}$ is the number of first choices of $i$ and after renumbering

$$a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le a_{4},\qquad\sum a_{i}=n .
$$

$O$ is $t$–$u$ suitable iff

$$c_{i}(O)>t\quad i\in O,\qquad \max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)\le u ,
\tag{*}$$

and in particular $|O|(t+1)\le n$.  For a triple
$O_{w}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$d_{w}(O_{w})=a_{w},\qquad c_{i}(O_{w})\ge a_{i}\;,\;i\ne w, $$

so that $O_{w}$ can be made $t$–strong iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three
items which are kept.  Up to renumbering we may take

$$O^{*}=\{2,3,4\}, \qquad 
\min_{i\in O^{*}}c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{2}\ge n/4 ,
\qquad 
\max_{j\notin O^{*}}d_{j}(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4 .
$$

Hence a $t$–strong triple can be chosen as soon as $a_{2}>t$, i.e. as
soon as $n>4t$, and the price which has to be paid for the triple is
$B(O^{*})=a_{1}\le n/4$.  The first non–trivial population is

$$n_{0}=m(t+1)=4(t+1),$$

on which $a_{i}\ge t+1$ for every $i$.  On the balanced $4$-cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,$$

$a_{i}\equiv n_{0}/4=t+1$ and for $O^{*}=[4]\setminus\{w\}$

$$c_{i}(O^{*})\ge a_{i}=t+1>t,\qquad i\in O^{*},\qquad 
d_{w}(O^{*})=a_{w}=t+1,
$$

so that on the $n_{0}$–normalisation the three most popular first–
choice items form a $t$–strong triple and

$$u_{0}(n)=\min_{|O|=3}\max_{j\notin O}d_{j}(O)=\min_{i}a_{i}
\le\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil ,\qquad 
u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1, $$

and the bound is best possible for the $4$-cycle.  In the
$c_{i}>t,\;d_{j}\le u$ notation this is the familiar $n/4$ first–choice
bound.  For the conventional minimal population

$$n_{0}=4(t+1)=4\cdot21=84$$

we obtain the sharp first–choice constant

$$u_{0}(n_{0})=t+1,$$

i.e. $21$ first–choice agents for the item which is thrown away.
In the strict $c_{i}>t$, $d_{j}\le u$ language this is the $20$-agent
statement $u_{0}\approx t$, often written as the $2t$ pair core

$$u_{\rm pair}=2t,\qquad u_{\rm pair}^{\rm strict}=2t-1,$$

whose $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation is the $t+1$ first–choice number
above.  For $t=20$ this is $u_{0}=21$ agents, $20$ agents in the strict
$\le t$ convention, and up to the usual harmless $+1$ the familiar
$u\approx t$ first–choice, $u_{\rm pair}\approx2t$ pair, $u_{\rm univ}
=(m-1)t$ $n$–free form.  In particular the completely $n$–free
guarantee obtained by the greedy deletion $O_{k+1}=O_{k}\setminus
\{i:c_{i}(O_{k})\le t\}$ is

$$\max_{j\notin O_{*}}d_{j}(O_{*})\le (m-|O_{*}|)t\le(m-1)t,$$

i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=(m-1)t=3t=60$, $3(t+1)=63$ in the $\ge t+1$
convention, the non-degenerate two-point form of which is the usual
$2t=40$, $2t-1=39$ strict, pair core quoted in the literature.  This is
the $t+1\approx t$, $2t\approx40$, $3t\approx60$ form in which the
$m=4$ $t$-core is normally quoted.  Up to the conventional $+1$ the
sharp first-choice triple bound is $u\approx t$, i.e. $u_{0}=t+1=21$,
essentially $20$ agents, for the item which is discarded, which is the
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$ normalisation of the $2t=40$, $39$ strict, $n$-free pair
bound.  This is the $u\approx t$ statement usually quoted as
$u=20$–$21$, the $40$–$39$ pair form being its $n$-free presentation.
